items.title: Bank Al-Maghrib muscle son arsenal contre les crises
items.description: La nouvelle loi n°87.21 renforce les outils dont dispose Bank Al-Maghrib pour intervenir en amont des difficultés bancaires et organiser, si nécessaire, la résolution d’un établissement sans solliciter systématiquement les finances publiques. La gestion des crises bancaires change de dimension. Avec la loi n°87.21, publiée au Bulletin officiel n°7533, le cadre juridique applicable aux établissements de crédit et à Bank Al-Maghrib est profondément remanié. Le texte introduit de nouveaux mécanismes permettant d’intervenir avant qu’une situation ne devienne irréversible et organise plus précisément le traitement d’une éventuelle défaillance. L’enjeu dépasse la seule surveillance prudentielle. Il s’agit désormais de disposer d’une architecture juridique permettant d’agir suffisamment tôt, de préserver les fonctions essentielles d’un établissement en difficulté et de limiter les conséquences d’une crise sur les déposants et la stabilité financière. Intervenir avant que la crise ne devienne irréversible La réforme renforce d’abord le dispositif d’intervention précoce. Bank Al-Maghrib peut notamment désigner un ou plusieurs administrateurs provisoires auprès d’un établissement de crédit. Leur mission peut aller de l’assistance aux organes de direction à l’exercice direct de leurs compétences lorsque la gravité de la situation le justifie. Dans ce dernier cas, les pouvoirs des organes de gestion et de contrôle sont suspendus au profit de l’administrateur provisoire. Celui-ci dispose également de prérogatives destinées à préserver les actifs de l’établissement. Avec l’autorisation de la Banque centrale, il peut notamment saisir le président du tribunal compétent afin de faire annuler certaines opérations réalisées au cours des six mois précédant sa désignation, lorsqu’elles ne relevaient pas de l’activité courante ou avaient pour objectif de soustraire des actifs. Le dispositif encadre parallèlement les conditions d’exercice de cette mission. Certaines opérations, notamment celles portant sur des biens immobiliers ou des participations, restent soumises à l’autorisation préalable de Bank Al-Maghrib. Les contrats en cours ne peuvent, de leur côté, être résiliés au seul motif du placement sous administration provisoire. L’administrateur doit en outre transmettre un rapport trimestriel à la Banque centrale sur l’évolution de la situation financière et la mise en œuvre des mesures de redressement. Sa mission cesse lorsque l’établissement est rétabli, lorsque sa situation est devenue irrémédiablement compromise ou lorsqu’il n’est plus en mesure d’exercer normalement ses fonctions. Autorité de résolution bancaire La réforme introduit également une autorité de résolution bancaire. Présidée par le wali de Bank Al-Maghrib, cette instance intervient pour les établissements dont une défaillance est susceptible d’affecter la stabilité de l’ensemble du système financier. Composée de huit membres ( deux magistrats désignés par le Conseil supérieur du pouvoir judiciaire, deux représentants du ministère chargé des Finances, deux représentants de Bank Al-Maghrib et deux membres indépendants ) elle dispose de compétences directement liées à la préparation et à la gestion des crises. Elle doit notamment examiner et adopter le plan préventif de résolution de chaque établissement concerné, décider de l’ouverture d’une procédure de résolution et arrêter les mesures nécessaires au traitement de la crise. L’activation du dispositif intervient lorsque les mesures de redressement ne permettent plus de rétablir la continuité et la viabilité de l’établissement, lorsque la poursuite de ses fonctions essentielles est menacée ou lorsque sa situation fait peser une menace immédiate sur la stabilité financière. Cette logique modifie ainsi l’approche de la défaillance bancaire. Plutôt que d’attendre qu’une crise atteigne un point de rupture, le nouveau cadre prévoit une procédure permettant d’organiser en amont les conditions de son traitement. Le financement de la résolution réorganisé La réforme touche également au financement des opérations de résolution. Le Fonds collectif de garantie des dépôts, dont la vocation première est de protéger les déposants, voit ses missions élargies. Il peut désormais contribuer au financement des mesures nécessaires au traitement d’une défaillance bancaire. Le recours aux ressources publiques n’est toutefois pas exclu. Le texte prévoit la possibilité d’un soutien exceptionnel de l’État en dernier ressort. L’objectif est ainsi de disposer de plusieurs leviers de financement avant d’envisager une intervention publique. Le texte final a par ailleurs été enrichi au cours de son examen parlementaire. Les amendements adoptés par la commission des Finances et du Développement économique ont notamment renforcé les exigences de gouvernance et de transparence liées à l’octroi et au retrait des agréments, en élargissant les situations liées à la transmission de données ou de déclarations inexactes ou trompeuses. Les parlementaires ont également précisé les notions relatives aux risques systémiques et à la stabilité financière, en renforçant leur articulation avec la protection de l’économie nationale. Le rôle du Fonds collectif de garantie des dépôts dans le financement des mesures de résolution a enfin été davantage encadré, dans une logique de mobilisation de plusieurs sources de financement. items.title: Death toll from Sokoto boat mishap hits 65
items.description: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto The death toll from the horrific boat mishap at Gorau Village in Goronyo Local Government Area of Sokoto State has risen to 65, with only 11 survivors so far accounted for, as grief, anger and renewed calls for urgent intervention spread across the state. The tragedy, which occurred on Thursday at the Gorau crossing point, has emerged as one of the deadliest recent waterway disasters in the country, leaving families devastated and communities mourning the loss of their loved ones. The latest casualty figure was recorded on Friday after rescue agencies resumed search operations suspended on Thursday evening because darkness and difficult conditions made further operations unsafe. At least 53 bodies had been recovered before the suspension of the operation, but the resumption of the search on Friday led to the recovery of additional bodies, pushing the confirmed death toll to 65. The National Inland Waterways Authority, NIWA, confirmed that 11 persons survived the mishap including the Village head Alhaji Na Batsami Gorau, while several of the recovered bodies were buried in accordance with Islamic rites as bereaved families and residents struggled to come to terms with the scale of the disaster. The tragedy has heightened concerns over the safety of Nigeria’s inland waterways, particularly in riverine communities where residents rely heavily on canoes and other boats for transportation, agricultural activities, trade and access to neighbouring communities. Rescue officials continued to comb the waterways around the Gorau crossing point in search of possible victims, although hopes of recovering more survivors had diminished considerably as the operation progressed. The Head of Operations, NEMA Sokoto Operations Office, Alhaji Tukur Abubakar, declined to comment on the latest casualty figure and directed all enquiries to the Sokoto State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA. Attempts to reach the Special Adviser to the Sokoto State Governor on SEMA, Alhaji Aminu Liman Bodinga, for further clarification proves impossible as his mobile telephone was switched off at the time of filing this tragic report. Reacting to the tragedy, the Chairman of the Governing Board of NIWA, Alhaji Mukhtar Shehu Shagari, described the incident as painful and devastating, extending condolences to the Sokoto State Government, Goronyo Local Government Council, traditional institutions and families of the victims. Shagari urged boat operators and passengers to comply strictly with established waterway safety regulations, stressing that tragedies of such magnitude must not become a recurring feature of inland water transportation in the country. Former Sokoto State Governor and Senator representing Sokoto South, Aminu Waziri Tambuwal, also expressed deep sorrow over the loss of lives and called for an immediate investigation into the circumstances surrounding the tragedy. Tambuwal said the investigation should establish both the immediate and remote causes of the accident and ensure that appropriate measures were taken to prevent a recurrence, insisting that the recurring loss of lives on Nigeria’s waterways could no longer be dismissed as an inevitable consequence of riverine transportation. But beyond the immediate circumstances of the boat mishap, the member representing Goronyo/Gada Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives, Hon. Bashir Usman Gorau, has raised a broader alarm over the condition of the Goronyo Dam and its tributaries, demanding urgent federal intervention to prevent further disasters. Gorau called on the Federal Government to commence the comprehensive desilting of Goronyo Dam and its tributaries, warning that decades of accumulated silt and sediments had significantly reduced the facility’s water-holding capacity and could worsen flooding and other water-related disasters in surrounding communities. According to the lawmaker, the dam, constructed by the Federal Government more than five decades ago, has accumulated enormous quantities of sediments over the years, thereby compromising its original capacity and threatening communities that depend on the water infrastructure. “A dam that was designed decades ago cannot continue to function effectively when its reservoir and waterways are choked with sediments. The capacity of Goronyo Dam has been seriously compromised, and the consequences are being felt every year by communities living downstream and around the dam,” Gorau said. He expressed concern that the continued deterioration of the dam and its tributaries could compound the vulnerability of communities during periods of heavy rainfall, potentially resulting in flooding, destruction of property, displacement and further loss of lives. Gorau described the accumulated sediments as a “clear and present danger” requiring immediate federal intervention, rather than waiting for disasters to occur before authorities mobilise emergency relief and rescue operations. He urged the Federal Government, relevant ministries and agencies responsible for water resources, dams and disaster management to declare the desilting of Goronyo Dam and its tributaries an emergency intervention and deploy the required technical expertise and resources without further delay. The lawmaker stressed that the exercise must go beyond the dam’s reservoir to include critical tributaries and waterways feeding the facility, arguing that only a comprehensive approach could address the underlying causes of the recurring flooding and waterway-related disasters in the area. “We cannot continue to wait until people are killed, communities are submerged and property worth millions is destroyed before we take action. Goronyo Dam has served the nation for over five decades; it now requires urgent rehabilitation and desilting to restore its capacity and protect the people. The time to act is now, before another life is lost,” Gorau declared. He further appealed to the Federal Government to combine the desilting programme with stronger waterway safety enforcement, improved emergency response mechanisms, provision of adequate life jackets, proper regulation of boat operations and sustained monitoring of vulnerable crossing points. The Goronyo tragedy has consequently reignited a national debate over the safety of Nigeria’s inland waterways and the need for government to invest in preventive infrastructure rather than continue to respond only after disasters have claimed lives. Goronyo communities, many of which depend on waterways for movement of people and agricultural produce, now face renewed uncertainty as residents demand concrete action to ensure that the latest tragedy does not become another statistic in Nigeria’s growing record of preventable waterway disasters. As Sokoto mourns the 65 victims, pressure is mounting on the Federal Government, NIWA, NEMA, SEMA and other relevant authorities to move beyond condolences and emergency responses by implementing lasting measures capable of safeguarding lives and livelihoods. items.title: Imran's sister files contempt plea over alleged violation of SC order on PTI founder's hospital transfer
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Dr Uzma Khan, the sister of PTI founder Imran Khan, approached the Supreme Court (SC) on Saturday seeking to initiate contempt proceedings against those responsible for violating its Aug 18 order for shifting the incarcerated premier to a private hospital in the federal capital. The petition, moved by Advocate Uzair Karamat Bhandari, also requested the SC to depute an officer of the court or appoint a local commission to ensure that Imran was immediately shifted to Shifa International Hospital for his medical examination in accordance with the Aug 18 order. Islamabad Chief Commissioner Islamabad, (retired) Lieutenant Sohail Ashraf, Interior Secretary Ahmed Raza Sarwar, Punjab Inspector General Prisons Mian Salik Jalal, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar were named as respondents in the petition. While all eyes were on Shifa International Hospital, a private medical facility, during the early hours of Friday, the government quietly moved Imran to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims) for a medical check-up in, ostensibly due to security concerns, following which he was taken back to Adiala jail. The PTI leadership and Uzma, who was present for the medical examination, had slammed the government’s conduct. The contempt plea filed by Uzma on Saturday urged the SC to initiate contempt proceedings against the respondents for their “wilful, deliberate and contumacious disobedience and violation” of the Aug 18 order. The petition contended that the court was being approached in light of the “non-compliance and brazen violations” by the respondents of the SC’s orders. “It is clear from the respondents’ own admissions that the court directions contained in Aug 18 order were violated,” it said. “The directions contained in the Aug 18 orders were clear, unambiguous, unequivocal and fully capable of implementation,” the petition said, adding they were issued in the presence of the Islamabad advocate general and the additional attorney general of Pakistan. “No portion thereof requires any further interpretation, clarification or modification,” the petition argued. It said that the respondents, being the officials responsible for putting the directions into effect, were under an absolute legal obligation to comply with the order “in letter and spirit”. “Needless to say, the mere filing of a review petition on the part of the chief commissioner does not affect the legal status of the court order and does not justify non-compliance with it,” the plea said. It said that even if a clarification or modification was required or there was apprehension of a security situation, an application needed to be filed. It said that the failure to shift Imran to Shifa International Hospital “leaves no manner of doubt that [the respondents] have consciously chosen to disregard and violate the Aug 18 court order”. It said that this was a case of deliberate and wilful disobedience and a violation of the order, interference with the process of law and obstruction of the judicial process. The petition said that the respondents’ conduct undermined the authority of the SC, adding that such conduct warranted cognisance by the court. The petition requested the SC to issue show-cause notices to the respondents and direct them to appear personally. The petition also requested to impose appropriate punishments against the respondents and direct to take all appropriate steps to implement the directions contained in the Aug 18 order for Imran’s medical examination.

items.title: La Belgique présente Hans Kluge comme candidat à la direction générale de l’OMS
items.description: Le gouvernement fédéral belge a proposé la candidature d'Hans Kluge au poste de directeur général de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS), a annoncé vendredi le médecin belge sur le réseau social X. « Je suis très honoré de la confiance que la Belgique me porte et suis reconnaissant de la chance qui m'est offerte d'assumer cette responsabilité importante », a commenté M. Kluge. Âgé de 57 ans, Hans Kluge occupe depuis 2020 les fonctions de directeur régional pour l'Europe auprès de l'OMS. Conformément aux règles en vigueur au sein de l'organisation, il démissionne de ses fonctions de directeur vu son statut de candidat. Le Belge a affirmé qu’il mettra cette période à profit pour s'entretenir avec les États membres de l'OMS, ses partenaires ainsi que le terrain pour échanger sur leurs attentes, leur vision d'avenir pour l'OMS et la santé globale. L'élection pour le remplacement du président sortant, l'Ethiopien Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, aura lieu lors de la 80e Assemblée mondiale de la santé, en mai 2027. Les États membres ont jusqu'au 24 septembre pour faire part de leurs candidats au poste. items.title: Huile d’olive tunisienne | Exportations en hausse de 55%
items.description: Selon les dernières données de l’Observatoire national de l’agriculture (Onagri) rapportées par l’agence Tap, il y a eu une évolution notable des performances du secteur de l’huile d’olive en Tunisie au cours des neuf premiers mois de la campagne actuelle, avec des quantités exportées record, atteignant 368 000 tonnes contre 236 900 tonnes durant la même période de la campagne précédente, soit une augmentation de 55,3 %. Selon un rapport publié vendredi 21 août 2026 par l’Onagri sur sa page Facebook officielle, ce dynamisme des exportations a eu un impact positif sur les recettes financières du pays : la valeur des exportations s’est élevée à 4 605,3 millions de dinars (MDT), enregistrant une croissance de 44,4 % par rapport à la campagne précédente (3 190 MDT). Cette hausse est portée par une demande mondiale croissante, notamment pour l’huile d’olive vierge extra, qui a représenté à elle seule 83,6 % du volume total exporté. Les exportations d’huile d’olive conditionnée ont également enregistré une progression de 50,8 %, les quantités exportées passant de 34 1000 tonnes à 51 500 tonnes ; elles représentent ainsi 14 % du volume total des exportations, contre 86 % pour l’huile d'olive exportée en vrac. La part des exportations d’huile d’olive conditionnée a atteint 18,6 % des recettes totales d’exportation au cours des neuf premiers mois de la campagne actuelle. Par ailleurs, le prix moyen de l’huile d’olive a augmenté de 1,4 % en juillet 2026 par rapport à la même période de la campagne précédente, passant de 12,97 dinars le kilogramme à 13,16 dinars ; les prix ont varié, selon les variétés, entre 8,22 et 17 dinars le kilogramme. Plus de 70 marchés À la fin du mois de juillet 2026, les exportations d’huile d’olive tunisienne étaient réparties sur plus de 70 pays, témoignant ainsi de la diversité des marchés extérieurs. Le marché de l’Union européenne absorbe la plus grande part des exportations, soit 57,1 %, avec en tête l’Espagne (32,1 %) et l’Italie (20 %). L’Amérique du Nord occupe la deuxième place avec une part de 24 %, répartie principalement entre les États-Unis (19,2 %) et le Canada (4,8 %). Les marchés asiatiques représentent 11,3 % du volume total des exportations, l’Arabie saoudite 4,6 %, la Jordanie 3,1 %, le marché africain 3,8 % et le marché égyptien 3,3 %. 673,4 MDT de recettes pour l’huile bio Concernant l’huile d’olive biologique, les quantités exportées au cours des neuf premiers mois de la campagne 2025/2026 ont atteint environ 51 200 tonnes, pour une valeur avoisinant les 673,2 MDT. La part de l’huile d’olive biologique conditionnée n'a pas dépassé 6,2 % du volume total des exportations de cette catégorie. Le prix moyen de l’huile d’olive biologique s’est établi à 13,16 dinars le kilogramme, oscillant entre 12,93 dinars le kilogramme pour l’huile «en vrac» et 16,56 dinars le kilogramme pour l’huile «conditionnée» . L’Italie arrive en tête des pays importateurs d’huile d’olive biologique tunisienne, avec une part de 38 % du volume total exporté, suivie par l’Espagne (26 %), les États-Unis (23 %) et la France (8 %). items.title: MLS fines Messi for striking opponent
items.description: Major League Soccer fined Inter Miami’s Argentine superstar Lionel Messi an undisclosed amount on Friday for slapping Philadelphia’s Quinn Sullivan on the back of the neck in the clubs’ 2-2 draw on Wednesday. The league’s disciplinary committee said it had levied the fine “for violating the league’s policy regarding hands to the face/head/neck of an opponent.” Miami’s Ian Fray was fined an undisclosed amount for the same infraction. It was late in stoppage time of a testy contest when Messi approached the center circle to confront Sullivan while the ball was in play in another area of the field. After a brief exchange, Messi took a swipe at Sullivan, who then squared up to the Argentine star in a fight-style stare-down. Referee Filip Dujic, who had his back turned during the incident, arrived to separate the players but did not show either of them a card. Dujic did send off Cavan Sullivan, younger brother and teammate of Quinn, and Miami’s Italian midfielder Yannick Bright after their stoppage time scuffle in Miami’s penalty area. AFP The post MLS fines Messi for striking opponent appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Dance, laughter as Vanguard’s ex-staff return home to launch book, dine, wine with the family
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku Last Wednesday was a day of overflowing joy for the patriarch of Vanguard Family, Sam Amuka-Pemu, widely referred and revered as Uncle Sam. The journalists he had mentored, nurtured and sent out into the world returned to say ‘Thank you.’ The air was heavy with memories, laughter and gratitude. It was a reunion that restored roots, revived bonds and reminded everyone of where it all began. Amid tributes and applause, Uncle Sam stood in quiet awe, honoured not just by the words spoken, but also by the lives his guidance had shaped. Indeed, it was a homecoming that rekindled nostalgia and renewed old bonds at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, the venue for the reunion of Vanguard Alumni and a book launch to mark 40 years of the newspaper. For over 40 years, many of the returning alumni had been away from their roots. Yet the moment they stepped in, the hall was filled with an unmistakable aura of reconnection. The joy was endless. Uncle Sam was not only elated and honoured as he reunited with his many “sheep” scattered across the world who once drank from his fountain of journalistic wisdom, but he was also moved to awe by the encomiums poured on him. The event, defined by memory, pride, and the enduring power of mentorship, drew friends of Vanguard, prominent personalities from the political, business, diplomatic, security and media sectors, as well as former and current members of the Vanguard family. In attendance were representative of former Head of State, General Ibrahim Babangida, (retd), Professor Mohammed Yahaya Kuta of the University of Ibadan; former Governors Olusegun Osoba, Rotimi Amaechi, and Peter Obi. Other dignitaries included Publisher of This Day Newspaper and founder of Arise News TV, Prince Nduka Obaigbena; the President of the Nigeria Labour Congress, Comrade Joe Ajaero, who is also a former staff of Vanguard; Laos State former Commissioner of Information, Steve Ayorinde; the Inspector General of Police, Olatunji Disu; media executives and numerous former staff of the company who testified to Uncle Sam’s kind-heartedness and human nature. Setting the tone for the evening, Osoba recounted Amuka’s journey in Nigerian journalism, including his role in establishing The Punch before founding Vanguard Newspaper in 1984. He said Amuka briefly left journalism for the fishery business after parting ways with The Punch, but soon returned to what he called his greatest passion. Osoba also praised Amuka for upholding Vanguard’s editorial independence, recalling that during the 2023 election campaign he had complained to the publisher that the APC was unhappy with the paper’s editorial stance. “Rather than interfere with the newspaper’s editorial decision, Amuka referred me to the editor, Eze Anaba. I was embarrassed,” he recalled, describing Amuka as “a generalissimo of journalism in Nigeria.” But beyond the long speeches and tributes to the man who mentored many of Nigeria’s “great pen pushers,” a major highlight of the event was the unveiling of a publication documenting key events, personalities and defining moments in Nigeria’s history through Vanguard’s coverage over four decades. The book reviewer, Mr Gbemiga Ogunnleye took the audience through the compelling story behind the making of Vanguard. He paid tributes to departed members of staff, stirring deep emotion in the hall. As he reeled out their names, silence fell over the venue in a solemn moment of remembrance. The book, which was originally meant to be presented to the public in 2024, when Vanguard clocked 40 years on the newsstands, documents significant events, personalities and milestones in Nigeria’s history through Vanguard’s reportage spanning four decades. According to the book reviewer, “It’s a fitting testament to what is possible when young men and women share the vision of a man determined to live his dreams. Young men and women left their comfort zones, leaving certainty for uncertainty, to partake in the vision of Uncle Sam. This book is a compelling account of the challenges and tribulations of the early years of Vanguard. “Not surprising, the book begins with a foreword by Uncle Sam’s friend of over 60 years and his colleague at Daily Times, Chief Segun Osoba, who aptly described his friend as a lucky man because It is not often that a person gets a second chance to succeed. Having got his fingers burnt in Punch, a good fortune smiled on him with a second chance in Vanguard”. After the book launch, the programme moved into another key segment: the reunion proper. Tagged ‘Meet and Greet of the Vanguard Alumni,’ members took turns introducing themselves to loud cheers and applause from the audience Sharing his experience as a former Vanguard staff, Chairman of Vanguard Media Alumni Association, Pastor Eyobong Ita, said the newspaper gave him an opportunity to build a career despite having no university education, journalism degree or formal journalism training when he joined the organisation. “I stand before you today to declare that Vanguard is a place where dreams come true. If you dare to dream, and you are privileged to join Vanguard newspapers, Vanguard is a place where dreams come true,’’ he said. The atmosphere was electric when Mr Peter Obi arrived at the event. His grand entrance was met with a standing ovation and a rousing rendition of the heroic Igbo song “Ebube Dike. For minutes, the hall rang with chants of ‘Okwute!’ He later gave a brief speech, praising Vanguard’s role in nation-building. The event ended on a high note, with the alumni members taking to the dancefloor. Amuka, who marked his 91st birthday on June 13 this year then summoned members of the Nigerian Guild of Editors in attendance to the dancefloor to dance to the glory of God. Indeed, it was a beautiful reunion of the Vanguard family filled with memories, fun and laughter. The post Dance, laughter as Vanguard’s ex-staff return home to launch book, dine, wine with the family appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Salvation in the bus!, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: There is a peculiar talent that governments sometimes acquire after years in office. It is the ability to mistake the symptom for the disease, to become so captivated by the manageable inconvenience that the genuine emergency fades into the wallpaper. Nations reveal themselves not only by the crises they endure, but by the crises they choose to confront. Some spend decades strengthening shields they’re and boarders because they understand that institutions outlive administrations. Others become fascinated by the theatre of governance, where visible action is mistaken for meaningful progress. The recent controversy surrounding the Federal Road Safety Corps amendment bill and its provision on preaching, hawking and trading inside commercial vehicles belongs to that familiar theatre. Whether the clause merely restated an existing prohibition or represented a fresh legislative impulse is almost incidental. The real story was never a preacher standing in the aisle of a commercial bus. It was our astonishing ability to invest enormous public energy in a question that sits comfortably on the margins while the centre continues to collapse. If anyone wishes to understand why that instinct has become so deeply Nigerian, they should spend a single morning inside a commercial bus. A woman climbs aboard carrying two bags of tomatoes. To everyone else, they are groceries waiting to become sales. To her, they are school fees, cough syrup, transport fare and, if the day is kind, a piece of meat in the evening pot. She settles into a cracked seat and instinctively draws her bags closer, knowing that tomatoes bruise almost as easily as profit. Around her sits a country held together by quiet endurance. An elderly man keeps opening a brown envelope to reassure himself that the hospital test results are still inside. Across from him, a university graduate studies the reflection on the dark screen of his phone, silently rehearsing answers for interviews that rarely become employment. A young mother rocks a sleepy child while calculating how long she can postpone buying another tin of infant formula. Beside the window, a mechanic with grease permanently worked into his fingernails sleeps with the heavy exhaustion of someone who has mistaken survival for rest. Nobody asks another passenger’s name. It is unnecessary. In a Nigerian commercial bus, introductions are a luxury. Everyone arrives carrying a private burden, and everyone leaves with it. The conductor slaps the body of the bus. “One more! One more!” It is the oldest fiction in public transportation. There is never one more. There are always four. The engine coughs awake and the bus joins the slow procession of a city already bargaining with itself. Hawkers drift effortlessly through the traffic selling bottled water, handkerchiefs, chargers and biscuits. Office workers weave between motorcycles with the urgency of people who know that lateness in Nigeria is often punished more severely than incompetence. Somewhere ahead, a broken-down tanker has converted an ordinary road into a lesson in collective patience. Inside the bus, the country’s parliament is already in session. “My landlord says the rent is going up again.” “My son graduated two years ago. He’s still looking.” “Rice was cheaper last week.” No one raises a voice. Hardship rarely requires volume. It simply settles into the empty spaces between ordinary conversations. The woman with the tomatoes says nothing. She is occupied by a mathematics that no university teaches. If she sells everything before noon, she can restock tomorrow. If prices rise again, she will buy fewer baskets. If her youngest daughter’s cough refuses to disappear, medicine will compete with school fees. If nothing unexpected happens, and in Nigeria that is always the most expensive assumption, perhaps tomorrow will resemble today. Then the bus crashes into a pothole. The tomatoes lurch forward. She catches them before they spill into the aisle. The old man instinctively shields his envelope. The graduate grips his phone. For a brief moment, every passenger reaches for the one fragile thing that cannot afford to break. At the next junction, a man rises from the back seat with a small Bible in his hand. His faded blue shirt has survived too many washings to remember its original colour. He smiles, clears his throat and begins softly. “My brothers and sisters…” Half the passengers already know how the story will unfold. Some bow their heads. Others continue staring through the window. The conductor keeps demanding exact change with unwavering commitment. The preacher speaks quietly about gratitude, uncertain journeys and the dangerous confidence of believing tomorrow has already made provision for us. When he finishes, he thanks the passengers, returns to his seat and becomes anonymous once again. The bus moves on, carrying not merely commuters, but a republic in miniature. In Part Two, I’ll pivot from this bus journey to the deeper political argument, showing why the real issue was never the preacher at all, before ending with a much more haunting conclusion built around the tomato seller. I think that’s where this version can rise from excellent to genuinely memorable. The bus offers a useful education for anyone trying to understand the country’s political imagination. A visitor spending his first day in Nigeria would leave with a catalogue of obvious national anxieties. He would see roads that consume more hours than distance should permit. He would hear conversations shaped by inflation, unemployment, rising rents and shrinking purchasing power. He would notice that almost every passenger is carrying a calculation invisible to everyone else, forever adding, subtracting and postponing. He would reasonably conclude that these are the questions occupying the full attention of those entrusted with governance. Then he would discover that one of the loudest public arguments concerns what should happen when someone begins preaching before the conductor has finished collecting transport fare. The bewilderment would be understandable. No society should object to conversations about courtesy in shared public spaces. Commuters deserve peace if they want it. Those who preach, trade or entertain inside commercial vehicles should exercise consideration for people who may be carrying grief, exhaustion or simply a desire for silence. Civilised societies are built on mutual respect. But proportion matters. The measure of a government’s seriousness is not whether it can regulate the small inconveniences of everyday life. It is whether it can summon the imagination and discipline to confront the larger forces that make those inconveniences feel unbearable in the first place. The woman carrying tomatoes does not board that bus wondering whether someone might preach before she reaches her destination. She wonders whether she will sell enough before the afternoon heat softens the fruit. The graduate is not consumed by the possibility of an unsolicited sermon. He is wondering whether another week will pass without the telephone call that changes his life. The elderly man is thinking about test results, not public order. Their burdens are older than the debate. They will almost certainly outlive it. That is the danger of symbolic politics. It creates the reassuring appearance of movement while leaving reality stubbornly where it has always been. It is easier to regulate behaviour than to repair institutions, easier to draft another rule than to rebuild an economy, easier to police the visible than to confront the slow, patient failures that quietly shape a nation’s destiny. History is full of governments that became remarkably efficient at organising appearances while neglecting foundations. They announced campaigns as factories closed. They enforced order as public confidence dissolved. They perfected the language of action while ordinary people perfected the art of endurance. Nigeria has never lacked regulations. It has too often lacked the institutions that make regulations meaningful. Perhaps that is why the commercial bus feels less like public transport than a moving census of deferred dreams. Every morning it gathers strangers whose lives would never otherwise intersect and reminds us that the country’s greatest common language is not ethnicity, religion or politics, but quiet perseverance. The accountant, the trader, the mechanic, the graduate and the widow may vote differently and pray differently, but they all understand the arithmetic of survival. That is also why the preacher is not really the central figure in this story. The tomato seller is. She never interrupted the sermon because survival had already become her liturgy. She needed no microphone to testify. Her gospel was written in prices that rose faster than her earnings, in children whose appetites ignored inflation, and in the fragile hope that tomorrow’s market might be kinder than today’s. When the bus finally reached her stop, she lifted her bags with the same care she had shown when she boarded, stepped into the morning and disappeared into the crowd. The preacher’s words remained inside the bus. Her work continued outside it. Perhaps that is where every public policy should ultimately be judged. Not by the applause it attracts, the headlines it generates or the impression of decisiveness it creates, but by a far simpler question. When the woman carrying the tomatoes gets off the bus, is her journey towards dignity any shorter than it was before? If the answer is no, then we may have regulated another symptom while leaving the disease untouched. Everything else is conversation. She still has tomatoes to sell. The post Salvation in the bus!, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Michael Tetteh Kwetey to contest NDC Greater Accra Regional Chairmanship
items.description: Michael Tetteh Kwetey, a former Constituency Secretary and Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), has announced his intention to contest the party’s Greater Accra Regional Chairmanship when nominations are opened. In a declaration of intent, Mr Kwetey said the decision followed calls from NDC supporters across the Greater Accra Region and beyond, urging him to offer himself for the position. He said the confidence expressed in his leadership was largely based on his years of dedicated service to the party in various capacities. “Comrades, I am here today in response to your calls. I have listened to you, reflected on your confidence in me, and heeded your call,” he said. Mr Kwetey, who recently contested as a Parliamentary Candidate aspirant in Ningo Prampram, said he would formally pick a nomination form once the process for the regional elections begins. He pledged to serve the party with “dedication, humility, integrity, and a strong sense of responsibility.” Expressing gratitude to party supporters for their continued confidence, Mr Kwetey said he remained committed to strengthening the NDC and contributing to its progress in the Greater Accra Region. He ended his declaration with the party slogan: “Long live the NDC. Long live the Greater Accra Region. Ɛyɛ Zu, Ɛyɛ Za.”

items.title: Tunisie | Le Mouvement Nafas appelle à la libération de Seifeddine Arfaoui
items.description: Le mouvement Nafas — qui a organisé des manifestations contre le régime de Kaïs Saïed le jeudi 20 août 2026 à Tunis — a publié un communiqué de soutien et de solidarité avec le militant Seifeddine Arfaoui, suite à son arrestation par les autorités. Selon certaines sources, cette arrestation fait suite aux slogans qu’il a scandés et qui ont été jugées offensantes et injurieuses pour le chef de l’Etat. Nous publions ci-dessous une traduction dudit communiqué. Le pouvoir autoritaire poursuit ses restrictions systématiques des droits et libertés, ainsi que la persécution des militants de la société civile, des acteurs politiques et des voix libres, dans une tentative désespérée d’intimider les citoyens et de les dissuader d’exercer leur droit à l’expression et de défendre leurs droits économiques et sociaux. Dans ce contexte, ce vendredi 21 août 2026, à la suite d’une campagne systématique sur les réseaux sociaux, le blogueur, défenseur des droits humains et militant du mouvement Nafas, Seifeddine Arfaoui, a été conduit au siège de la Brigade de lutte contre la criminalité à El Gorjani pour y être interrogé. Après consultation du ministère public, celui-ci a ordonné sa garde à vue pour une durée de 48 heures, en raison d’une publication sur sa page Facebook personnelle reprenant des slogans scandés lors de la manifestation «Nafas» du 20 août 2026. Il s’agit de la deuxième arrestation au sein du mouvement Nafas, après celle du journaliste Zied El Heni le 28 avril 2026, également intervenue à la suite d'une publication sur sa page Facebook personnelle. Au vu de ce qui précède, le mouvement Nafas : 1- exprime son soutien total et inconditionnel au militant Seifeddine Arfaoui, exige sa libération et l’abandon de toute poursuite à son encontre, ainsi que la fin des poursuites visant les personnes exprimant leurs opinions et les militants de la société civile et du monde politique pour l’exercice de leurs droits légitimes ; 2- réitère son refus de voir l’exercice des droits et libertés ainsi que la participation à des mouvements civiques pacifiques servir de motifs de poursuites judiciaires, ou voir les appareils de l’État instrumentalisés pour intimider les militants et dissuader les citoyens d’exprimer leurs positions et de participer à des actions civiques pacifiques ; 3- fait part de sa conviction que la situation de Seifeddine Arfaoui est indissociable du climat général dans lequel la liberté d’expression, les positions dissidentes et l’engagement civique sont désormais exposés à la criminalisation et aux poursuites. Défendre Seifeddine revient à défendre le droit de chaque Tunisien et de chaque Tunisienne à s’exprimer, à exprimer des opinions divergentes, à participer à la vie publique et à manifester pacifiquement. Nous refusons que des publications sur les réseaux sociaux se transforment en chefs d’accusation, que l’expression d’une opinion devienne un délit et que l’engagement citoyen pacifique serve de motif à une arrestation. Si ces pratiques visent à effrayer les gens et à les réduire au silence, nous affirmons que la répression et l’intimidation ne feront que renforcer notre détermination à exercer notre droit à l’expression, à la critique et à la contestation pacifique. Liberté pour Seifeddine Arfaoui. Liberté pour Zied El Heni. Liberté pour les prisonniers d’opinion et les prisonniers politiques. Communiqué traduit de l’arabe. L’article Tunisie | Le Mouvement Nafas appelle à la libération de Seifeddine Arfaoui est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Father ditches 7-year-old for hours to climb mountain
items.description: A man left his seven-year-old son behind for hours on Japan’s Mount Fuji while continuing the climb, resulting in a stern warning from authorities, police and local media reported. The boy was found alone on a hiking route on Thursday and taken into police custody, a local police officer in the Shizuoka region told AFP on Saturday. The child told his father he was tired at the sixth station of the mountain, which is located at an altitude of more than 2,000 metres (6,500 feet), local SBS TV reported. As his older brother had gone on ahead, the seven-year-old’s father told him to “wait here” and carried on hiking with his other son, according to SBS. TV Asahi said that the boy was told to wait for eight hours with only snacks and a soft drink and no money, citing staff at a mountain hut who alerted police to his presence. Officers contacted the father who was at the eighth station and handed the boy over to him when he returned. The police officer told AFP that officers gave the man a telling-off for leaving the child behind. The father reportedly apologised to the police, admitting the act was careless. AFP The post Father ditches 7-year-old for hours to climb mountain appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Las lluvias torrenciales provocan inundaciones en bajos y calles en Torredembarra y El Vendrell
items.description: La lluvia se ha cebado esta madrugada con la costa Daurada, en Tarragona, donde los municipios de Torredembarra, El Vendrell, Creixell y Roda de Berà (en las comarcas del Tarragonès y Baix Penedès) han recibido precipitaciones de entre 140 y hasta 200 litros por metro cuadrado, de los que 100 han caído en solo tres horas. Protección Civil ha explicado que los servicios de emergencia recibido 192 avisos relacionados con la tormenta por inundaciones de calles y bajos y personas atrapadas en coches. Se han evacuado 300 personas de un camping de Roda de Berà y unos 150 jóvenes de una discoteca de El Vendrell. El SEM ha atendido a tres personas de una familia de Roda de Berà por la caída de un muro, de las que una está herida crítica y está trasladada al hospital de Tarragona. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Seyi Vibez bows to pressure, after Hilda Baci threatens with lawsuit
items.description: By Benjamin Njoku & Tony-Okafor Favour Street pop star Seyi Vibez has deleted social media posts about celebrity chef Hilda Baci hours after receiving a legal warning threatening a lawsuit. The move comes amid an ongoing feud between the singer and his former label, Dapper Music, owned by Damilola Akinwunmi, popularly known as Dapper. Seyi Vibez, with ex-Dapper Music acts Shallipopi and T.I Blaze, had publicly accused the label of royalty disputes and alleged missing funds to the tune of N1 billion. In the heat of the exchange on X, Seyi Vibez made allegations against Hilda Baci, Dapper’s girlfriend. He claimed the music executive used money from their catalogue to fund Hilda’s cosmetic surgery, and also made disparaging remarks about her food business. Hilda, through her lawyers, responded with a cease-and-desist letter. She described the posts as defamatory and demanded that Seyi Vibez take them down and issue a public apology, or face legal action. “We hereby demand that upon receipt of this letter, you immediately remove and permanently delete the above referenced publications together with any other statement, post, comment, image, video and repost,” the letter read. The lawyers further demanded: “Issue a clear and unequivocal public apology and retraction in respect of the offending publications, to be published prominently and contemporaneously across all your social media accounts.” Following the warning, Seyi Vibez deleted all posts referencing Hilda Baci. As of press time, he is yet to issue the demanded public apology. Seyi Vibez signed with Dapper Music in 2022. He announced his exit in September 2024 and now describes himself as an “Independent artist.” The post Seyi Vibez bows to pressure, after Hilda Baci threatens with lawsuit appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Abike Ilu: ‘My drum hairstyle is my identity and mission to preserve Yoruba culture’
items.description: By Ishola Balogun She is impossible to miss in a crowd. Cultural entertainer and drummer Abike Ilu has a unique hairstyle in the image of a talking drum which has become her signature hairstyle. For Abike, the look is not just about style. It is a statement of identity and a mission to keep Yoruba heritage alive. “The drum-inspired hairstyle is more than a fashion statement; it is my identity and a symbol of my passion for Yoruba culture,” she said in a chat. “As a talking drummer, I wanted something that immediately tells people who I am and what I represent before I even perform. Maintaining it requires time, commitment, and resources, but I see it as an investment in my brand. It has sparked conversations, made me easily recognizable, and helped people remember me wherever I go. Many now identify me simply by that unique look. So yes, it has achieved its purpose. Abike Ilu describes herself as a cultural entertainer, talking drummer, and performer whose core mission is to preserve and promote Yoruba heritage through music and stagecraft. Her sound, she explains, is a fusion of ancestral rhythms and contemporary presentation. “My style blends traditional talking drum rhythms with contemporary sounds and modern stage presentation. This allows me to connect with older audiences who appreciate tradition and younger generations who enjoy modern entertainment. I believe culture should evolve without losing its originality, and that is exactly what my music represents. It is Afro-cultural”, she said. The drummer has been busy on the circuit in recent months. Her performances have spanned cultural festivals, weddings, corporate events, community celebrations, and social gatherings. She has also leveraged online platforms and media content to reach audiences beyond live shows. For Abike, each drumbeat is both entertainment and advocacy, a way to ensure that Yoruba tradition remains visible, relevant and exciting for new generations. In an industry where young talents often struggle for recognition, Abike Ilu has chosen a path where culture is the brand, the drum is the voice, and heritage is the message. The post Abike Ilu: ‘My drum hairstyle is my identity and mission to preserve Yoruba culture’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Mahama disappointed by US opposition to UN slavery resolution
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has expressed disappointment with the decision by the United States to vote against a landmark United Nations resolution recognising the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as the gravest crime against humanity. Speaking in an interview with TRT World on Friday, August 21, President Mahama said he had not expected the United States to oppose the resolution because, in his view, the country should not be regarded as the principal party responsible for the transatlantic slave trade. “I was disappointed that they did because I don’t hold the US accountable for slavery,” he said. According to the President, most of the enslaved Africans taken to what became the United States were transported there by European powers at a time when the United States itself was still a colony. He, however, acknowledged that slavery continued in the United States after independence and was only abolished following the Civil War. “Even though after the abolition and after the United States became an independent country, slavery continued until the Civil War was fought and that eventually freed the slaves in the US,” he said. President Mahama said that while the United States derived significant economic benefits from slavery, including infrastructure development, he did not believe the country should bear the same historical responsibility for the transatlantic slave trade as the European powers that organised and facilitated the trafficking of Africans to the Americas. “I don’t think that they should bear the guilt, in a certain sense, for it because I would have thought that the European countries that brought the slaves there would feel more adverse to the resolution,” he said. He said he was therefore concerned that the United States voted against the resolution while European countries with direct historical links to the slave trade chose to abstain. “Even they abstained,” he noted. The comments come months after Ghana secured a historic victory at the UN General Assembly when 123 countries voted in favour of the resolution on March 25, 2026. The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against it, while 52 countries, including Britain and European Union member states, abstained. The resolution, spearheaded by President Mahama in his capacity as the African Union Champion for advancing justice and the payment of reparations, also calls for good-faith dialogue on reparatory justice and the restitution of cultural property. It is not legally binding but carries significant political and moral weight. The vote represented a major milestone in Ghana’s campaign to place reparatory justice for slavery and its enduring consequences at the centre of the international agenda. The transatlantic slave trade forcibly removed millions of Africans from the continent between the 15th and 19th centuries, with the effects of enslavement continuing to shape debates on racial inequality, economic disparities, historical justice and restitution. President Mahama has maintained that the reparations campaign is not intended simply to reopen historical wounds but to promote truth, healing, reconciliation and practical measures to address the enduring consequences of slavery. At a high-level consultative conference in Accra in June, he said the pursuit of reparatory justice should move beyond resolutions towards concrete action. The European Union, in explaining its abstention at the UN vote, said it condemned the slave trade but had concerns about the resolution’s legal formulations, including claims for reparations and the application of international law to historical events. Ghana’s reparations campaign is expected to remain a major component of the country’s international diplomacy as the government works with African and diaspora partners to translate the UN resolution into practical measures for reparatory justice.

items.description: Elle s’appelle Sihem Djoudi, a fait ses études de médecine en Algérie et vient d’être nommée directrice générale de l'Équipe de santé familiale communautaire Montfort de l’Ouest d’Ottawa, au Canada . Cette structure est une clinique dont l’objectif est d’offrir en français des soins de santé primaires à la population de l’Ouest de la capitale canadienne. Une distinction méritée pour l’excellence de son parcours. Juste avant cette promotion, Sihem Djoudi occupait les fonctions de chargée de projet pour Collèges Ontario et de coordinatrice en développement des apprentissages au Collège La Cité. Elle a également enseigné, à temps partiel, à l’Université d’Ottawa, la capitale du Canada. Sihem Djoudi, une diplômée de l’Université d’Annaba nommée à la tête d’une clinique au Canada Sihem Djoudi est détentrice d’un doctorat en médecine obtenu à l’Université Badji Mokhtar, Annaba, ainsi que d’une maîtrise en technologie éducative et d’un diplôme d’études supérieures spécialisées de l’Université Laval. Ce brillant médecin cumule plus de 18 ans d’expérience dans les domaines de la santé, de l’enseignement postsecondaire et du développement organisationnel. Son engagement envers l’excellence en enseignement et l’innovation lui a ouvert la voie du couronnement. En 2016, le Dr Sihem Djoudi a reçu un prix en reconnaissance de son excellent parcours en tant que professeur des écoles interdisciplinaires des sciences de la santé. En 2023, le Prix du Mérite collégial pour l’excellence et l’innovation au collège La Cité lui a été remis. Une consécration méritée À l’occasion de sa nomination, le médecin algérien a déclaré : « C’est un privilège de contribuer à bâtir cette nouvelle organisation et de participer concrètement à l’amélioration de l’accès aux soins primaires en français dans l’Ouest d’Ottawa. » Dr Djoudi a exprimé son souhait, avec « l’équipe, les partenaires et la communauté, de bâtir une clinique accessible, collaborative et durable, où les besoins des patients-e-s sont au cœur de nos décisions et où chaque personne reçoit des soins humains et de grande qualité ». L’Équipe de santé familiale communautaire Montfort de l’Ouest d’Ottawa a été créée par l’Hôpital Montfort, la Coopérative multiservices francophone de l’Ouest d’Ottawa (CMFO) et le Conseil des écoles publiques de l’Est de l’Ontario (CEPEO), selon le site de l’hôpital canadien. L’article Sihem Djoudi, médecin algérienne, nommée à la tête d'une nouvelle clinique au Canada est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: 3.5m missing births:: How hospitals can close Nigeria’s registration gap
items.description: … Experts add: Register them where they are born By Chioma Obinna The first cry came, then the rush of hands. A newborn baby girl had just entered the world. While nurses attended to the mother and cleaned the baby, Emmanuel Joseph was already thinking beyond the excitement of fatherhood. He wanted his daughter to exist not only in his family, but also in the records of the country. Within minutes of his wife’s delivery, Joseph walked out of the labour area in search of the nurse in charge. “I asked if they had a desk where I could register the birth of my child,” he told Good health weekly. The nurse was surprised. “She asked if I really had a name for my child because the child would not be registered if I did not have a name. I told her yes.” Joseph was directed to a National Population Commission, NPC, registration unit within the hospital. There, another surprise awaited the registrar. “They were also surprised that I came for a child that the nurses were still busy cleaning up,” he said. But the registrar quickly got to work. A chair was provided, a form brought out and Joseph completed the necessary details. His daughter was registered. Free of charge. Before the family left the hospital, Joseph had in his hands what could become one of the most important documents in his daughter’s life — her birth certificate. “I know the importance of birth registration and what it means for a child. It shows that the child is a Nigerian and can be budgeted for and counted. She will need it all through her life,” he said. For Joseph, the experience was simple. For millions of Nigerian children, however, getting that first legal identity remains anything but simple. Across Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti and Edo states, an estimated 3.5 million children are without birth certificates, according to officials reports. These children are not missing and not necessarily abandoned. But they are living in homes, going to hospitals, attending clinics and growing up within communities but whose births may never have been entered into the official records of the country. In the words of Chief of UNICEF Lagos Field Office, Celine Lafoucriere: “They are children who are alive, at home, loved by their families, but completely invisible to their state and the country. “Some are in cities. Some are in villages. Some were born in hospitals and still never got registered. The gap is everywhere.” The contradiction is stark. A child may be born inside a health facility, surrounded by doctors, nurses, midwives and health workers, yet leave that same facility without a legal identity. That is the gap health facilities could help close. The delivery room as the first registration point. Hospitals, maternity centres and primary healthcare facilities occupy a unique position in the life of a newborn. They know when a baby is born. They know where the child was born. They have access to the mother, father or caregiver at one of the few moments when the entire family is physically present. They are therefore potentially the most strategic entry points for universal birth registration. According to experts, there was need to make birth registration part of routine maternal and newborn care, just as immunisation, weighing, postnatal checks and other essential services are integrated into the continuum of care. The civil registration system itself recognises this opportunity. One of the key accelerators identified for scaling up legal identity services is the integration of birth registration with primary healthcare services, alongside decentralisation, digitalisation, data interoperability and social mobilisation. The strategy envisages birth registration becoming an integral component of PHC services and expanding registration points to wards and health facilities. The logic is compelling. Instead of asking a mother who has just delivered a baby to make another journey to a distant registration centre, the registration service comes to the place where the birth has already been recorded. Instead of relying on parents to know that registration is free, health workers can tell them. Instead of waiting weeks or months, registration can begin before the mother leaves the facility. And instead of treating birth registration as a bureaucratic afterthought, it becomes part of protecting the child from the moment of birth. A mother’s experience Duke Juliet, a mother of two, understands the value of that document. “I just wanted to do a birth certificate for my child. Because I know that it’s very important,” she said. Her experience was largely seamless. She filled the form, submitted it and received the certificate without paying. When she later returned for immunisation, she was informed that the document was ready. Her experience with her first child was less straightforward. At one point, she had to redo the registration because the handwritten document was not ready for printing. The newer process, she said, was faster. “This one didn’t take up to a month. This one came out. There was no money,” she said. For Juliet, the lesson for other mothers is clear: information must follow women into the health system. “For other women, I think that once they go for immunization and all, they will be informed.” For Juliet, every antenatal clinic, every delivery room, every postnatal clinic, every immunisation session and every PHC visit could become an opportunity to ask one simple question: “Has this child been registered?” Where the system works, and where it breaks At on of the Primary Healthcare in Sangotedo, area of Lagos, the transition from paper to digital birth registration is already exposing both the promise and the weaknesses of the new system. According to Mr. Gabriel Aboton-Philip, NPC Registrar-in-Charge of Sangotedo, paper registration was officially discontinued from July 1, 2026, with registration moving online. The digital system, he said, has been welcomed by more educated parents. But for families in surrounding communities, the transition has exposed another layer of exclusion. The first obstacle is the National Identification Number, NIN. “Many of the mothers or the fathers don’t have NIN,” Aboton-Philip said. He recalled spending four days at the registration point for a free online registration exercise for children aged zero to five. Seventy-six people submitted their details. Only 46 were successfully registered. In some cases, parents provided NINs but their information could not be retrieved on the system. Then comes another familiar problem, connectivity. “When we register sometimes, when it gets to the point of submitting, sometimes it delays,” he said. The problem, he explained, is internet connectivity. The registrar therefore developed a workaround. Instead of keeping mothers waiting indefinitely, his team collects their details on a form and contacts them when necessary. “With good network, within five minutes, you are done with your registration. But if there are network challenges, sometimes it takes as long as 10 to 15 minutes, dealing with one person,” he said. The lesson is uncomfortable but important. Digitalisation can make birth registration faster, cheaper and more accessible. But digitalisation without reliable connectivity, functioning identity databases and trained personnel can simply move the barriers from a paper desk to a computer screen. Invisible barriers For families who fail to register their children, the reasons are not always neglect. Sometimes it is distance. Sometimes money. Sometimes language. Sometimes ignorance. Sometimes a lack of registration centres. Sometimes a parent does not understand why the document matters until the child urgently needs it. Speaking at a birth registration media dialogue in Lagos, the UNICEF Child Protection Specialist, Mr. Denise Onoise, identified limited accessibility, inadequate registration centres, long distances, language barriers, inefficient registration processes and insufficient financial, human and material resources as major obstacles. He noted that the burden is not only the official cost of registration. Families may also spend money travelling to registration points, lose income by taking time away from work, make repeated journeys and endure poor-quality services. “The problem is compounded in hard-to-reach areas and among disadvantaged population groups,” he said. This is why the hospital could be more than a place where a child is delivered. It could be the first gateway to citizenship. The price of being invisible. A birth certificate is often dismissed as a piece of paper that can be obtained later. But that paper represents much more. It establishes a child’s legal identity, name, gender, place and date of birth and provides information governments need for planning health, education, housing and social protection programmes. For UNICEF’s Lafoucriere: “A birth certificate is not a piece of paper. It is a child’s ticket into school. It is what allows a doctor to put a name on a patient file. It is how a family proves their child is theirs.” Without it, she warned, a child may face difficulties proving identity later in life, including accessing passports, voting and inheritance. The consequences can become even more dangerous for vulnerable children. Further, Onoise in his presentation, further identified risks ranging from exclusion from education, healthcare, social protection and justice systems to child marriage, child labour, trafficking, abuse, exploitation and family separation. Children in marginalised, underserved and hard-to-reach communities are particularly exposed. In other words, failure to register a birth does not merely create an administrative inconvenience. It can create a lifetime of vulnerability. NIN hurdle Nigeria’s move towards digital birth registration is also bringing the country’s identity systems face-to-face with one another. The current system requires parents to provide NIN details, while the birth registration process is designed to link the child to the national identity framework. Registrars told parents that registration for children aged zero to five is free and that parents should ensure their NIN information is correct before registration. The registrar also explained that the child must be physically present for capturing and that the system generates a NIN for the child. That integration could eventually create a seamless identity chain from birth to adulthood. But the Sangotedo experience shows why the chain must be as strong as its weakest link. If a mother does not have a NIN, the child’s registration may stall. If the NIN database does not return the parent’s details, registration may stall. If the internet fails, registration may stall. If there are too few registrars, registration may stall. And if the family lives far from a registration point, they may never start. The answer, therefore, is not simply to digitise. It is to bring the entire system closer to families. Experts say a registration desk beside the weighing scale would bridge gaps and ensures infants are given immediate legal identity. The case for integration with healthcare is already contained in the reform agenda. The proposed approach includes decentralising services to local governments and establishing more registration points at ward and health-facility levels. It also calls for stronger interoperability between civil registration, health and identity management systems. Imagine a mother arriving at a PHC for her baby’s immunisation. The nurse checks the child’s vaccination card. The health worker asks whether the birth has been registered. If not, the mother is immediately referred to an NPC registrar stationed within the facility or connected digitally to the registration system. The registrar verifies the parents’ details. The baby is captured. The birth is registered. The NIN is generated. The certificate is issued. One visit. One integrated system. One less child invisible to government. That is the promise. But the reality remains unfinished. However, according to Onoise on lessons learned from civil registration efforts showed that community-based registration expanded coverage and helped identify previously unregistered children. Digital registration improved efficiency and data quality, while interoperability strengthened coordination. He further revealed major weaknesses such as health-facility interoperability had stalled at the profiling stage, with none of 371 targeted facilities live despite completed training. The birth notification pipeline had recorded zero notifications in the reporting year, while certificate issuance lagged behind registration — 120,469 certificates issued against 443,162 registrations. That is the unfinished business. The delivery room is ready. The technology is emerging. The parents are already there. What is missing is a system capable of connecting all three. From paper to a national identity Nigeria’s civil registration architecture remains fragmented, with different agencies collecting identity-related information for different purposes. The National Identity Management Commission manages NIN; NPC handles population and civil registration data; immigration manages passports; the Federal Road Safety Corps manages driver’s licences; the Central Bank of Nigeria manages BVN, while INEC handles voter registration, among others. The fragmentation means critical child-related services such as school enrolment, immunisation and child justice do not yet operate through one unified identity system linked to birth registration. The Partnership Compact involving NPC, the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, NIMC, UNICEF and Barnksforte Technologies Limited is designed to tackle some of these weaknesses through harmonisation, decentralisation, stronger infrastructure and universal access. Under the proposed arrangement, NPC would manage the national birth and death registration system and work with local governments; ALGON would support implementation at local level and establish additional registration centres; NIMC would ensure identity-system integration and prompt NIN assignment; while UNICEF would provide technical, financial and technological support. The ambition is bigger than issuing certificates. It is about building a child-centred identity system that follows a Nigerian from birth through the services and opportunities that define life. A child born today should not have to become an adult before the country can prove that the child exists. The health system can change that. The first opportunity may come within minutes of birth. Joseph’s daughter is proof that when the system is available, when the parent understands its value and when the registrar is within reach, registration can happen before the family even leaves the hospital. His story should not be an exception. It should be the standard. Because every newborn arrives with more than a name chosen by parents. Every child arrives with a right to identity. And perhaps the most powerful place to begin protecting that right is where life itself begins — in the delivery room. The challenge now is to ensure that no mother walks out of a Nigerian hospital holding her newborn, while the country has yet to record that the child was ever born. Explaining how the e- birth registration works, the Lagos State Director of the National Population Commission, Sherifdeen Kekere-Ekun Mr Kekere-Ekun emphasized that birth registration is now fully free for children between 0 to 5 years. “We are no longer doing that handwritten registration. It has been phased out. We are now using digitalized one. This is digitalized birth certificate for your child. 0 to 5 years old is free. When you want to register your child, you must come with your NIN. Your NIN or your husband’s NIN. And make sure that the name is correct. The name on the NIN and the name that is going to be on the child’s birth certificate is correct. All the information, you have to give it to the registrar in charge to register your child. You are not paying 0 to 5 years. So once your child is above 5 years and you didn’t register, it’s called late registration. That is when you have to make payment. And the payment is N5,000. And you must provide an email to be able to log in. The old one is still valid. If you have registered the old one before 1st July, 2026, it’s still valid. You can still make use of it. But that’s not what we call it. We issue that manual only.” “For mothers, if you don’t want to change your name for your parents’ name and you want to still maintain your father’s name, it’s still okay. So whatever name that you have on your NIN is what is going to be applicable, to be applied on this birth certificate. So once there is a mistake on your NIN, you have to correct it before coming to the birth registration office. But if you want to change your husband’s name, there’s no problem. You have to make that correction before coming to the birth certificate office. Normally it takes 3 days. That is 72 hours. So that the NIN of your child will be applied.” “It also has a tracking eye that you can see here. You have to bring your baby when coming to register. You must come with your baby for capturing. Pictures are not acceptable when you are coming to register the baby.” Explaining some of the hitches, he said the NIN could not be confirmed or unable to submit, it may delay registration. He charged the media to move beyond reporting statistics and government activities by taking the birth registration message directly to parents and caregivers in communities. He stressed that accurate registration of births was also essential for effective governance, as reliable demographic data would enable government to determine the number and distribution of children and plan adequately for education, healthcare, social protection and other services. The post 3.5m missing births:: How hospitals can close Nigeria’s registration gap appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: PM Shehbaz directs authorities to provide financial assistance to flood-hit families
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday directed the relevant authorities to provide financial support to families affected by the recent monsoon rains and floods, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. The statement said that the premier issued the directions while chairing a meeting on the recent monsoon rains and floods and the damage caused. During the meeting, he directed that financial assistance be provided to the families of those who had lost their lives in the floods as well as to those whose homes had been partially or completely destroyed, the statement said. He instructed that restoration of the power supply and the rehabilitation of roads be completed as soon as possible, it added. He further directed the relevant federal ministers and secretaries to visit the affected areas, assess the damage, initiate rehabilitation work and expedite relief activities. PM Shehbaz ordered that essential food items and other relief supplies be delivered as soon as possible to the areas that had so far remained inaccessible. He also directed the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and the Provincial District Management Authorities (PDMAs) to remain fully prepared in view of the possibility of further rains and flooding. The statement said that during the meeting, the prime minister was briefed on the effects of monsoon in the current year and the update on relief activities taken by the NDMA and provinces. In the briefing, he was told that flood affectees across the country had been shifted to safer areas in a timely manner. PM Shehbaz was further informed that over all 615 tonnes of relief goods had been dispatched to affected areas, while measures were being taken to send more relief items to these areas, the statement said. He was also told that work on rehabilitating infrastructure in areas affected in Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir was ongoing. Early warning systems were also operational in the northern areas, the meeting was told. The systems had enabled the timely evacuation of several citizens to safe locations before the floods, it added. According to NDMA , 164 people have died in Pakistan between June 26 and August 21 during the ongoing monsoon season. On Friday, the Pakistan Met­­­­­eorological Department forecast a fresh spell of rain, wind and thundershowers across the country’s upper and central regions through the weekend, warning of potential urban and flash flooding. According to the Met Office, continuous monsoon currents are penetrating upper and central parts of Pakistan, alongside a westerly wave, bringing downpours from Aug 22 (today) to Aug 23 with occasional gaps. Rain, wind and thunderstorms with isolated heavy downpours are expected across Punjab’s major cities and divisions, including Lahore, Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Sargodha, Faisalabad and Multan. In KP, downpours are expected across the Hazara, Malakand, Peshawar, Mardan, Kohat and Dera Ismail Khan divisions. The weather system will also affect the entire Gilgit-Baltistan region and the Kashmir region, including Muzaffarabad and Mirpur. While Sindh and Balochistan will mostly remain hot and humid, isolated showers are expected in Balochistan’s Kalat and Zhob divisions.
