items.title: Return our IDPs to their homes before ranching, Benue leaders tell FG
items.description: By Peter Duru, Makurdi The three major socio-cultural organisations in Benue State have kicked against the Federal Government’s proposed pilot ranching scheme in Benue, state, insisting that the safe return and resettlement of displaced persons in the state must precede any land allocation for ranches. Read Also: Plateau to return IDPs to ancestral homes when safe — Mutfwang The leaders, who are the Presidents General of the Mzough U Tiv (MUT), Ochetoha k’Idoma, OKI and Omi Ny’Igede, ONI, said while they were not opposed to modern ranching, the policy must not be imposed on communities or implemented at the expense of displaced farmers and food production. President General of MUT Worldwide and Chairman of the Benue Socio-Cultural Organisations, Air Commodore Titus Agbecha (retd), stated this at a press conference attended by President General of Ochetoha k’Idoma, Prof. Yakubu Ochefu, and President General of Omi Ny’Igede, Daniel Omeno. Agbecha said the organisations received the Federal Government’s ranching proposal with “mixed feelings,” noting that ranching could help reduce herders’ incursions and improve food security if properly implemented. He however, said the peculiar security and humanitarian situation in Benue made it inappropriate to embark on large-scale land allocation for ranches before displaced communities were returned to their ancestral homes. According to him, “We currently have over 500,000 Benue people living in Internally Displaced Persons, IDP, Camps across Benue state. They have no home to return to, no shelter, no farms and no livelihood.” He described it as unjust to discuss new land use for ranches when “the owners of the land are still refugees in their own state.” The retired Air Commodore also alleged that several Benue communities had remained under siege for more than five years, with villages attacked and residents killed or displaced. “Establishing ranches under this atmosphere will be seen as rewarding violence and dispossession,” he warned, calling for comprehensive mediation, restoration of occupied communities and justice for victims before the scheme is introduced. The socio-cultural organisations further cautioned that large-scale land acquisition could threaten food production in Benue, which remains one of Nigeria’s major food-producing states. “Benue remains the food basket of the nation. Any programme that involves large-scale land acquisition must not undermine food production,” Agbecha said. The groups consequently urged the Federal Government to make the safe return and resettlement of all Internally Displaced Persons a priority, insisting that “peace must precede policy.” They also demanded genuine consultation, consent and compensation for host communities before any ranching project is undertaken. “We are not against modern ranching, but it must be voluntary, community-driven and must not displace food production,” Agbecha said. He appealed to Benue residents to remain calm and law-abiding, assuring that the socio-cultural organisations would continue to engage relevant authorities through dialogue. “Benue is the food basket of the nation. For Nigeria to be food secure, Benue farmers must first be secure on their land,” he added. The post Return our IDPs to their homes before ranching, Benue leaders tell FG appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘Gunmen went from house to house, killing people who were sleeping’ – Survivors of Plateau night of horror
items.description: *Over 24 dead, homes burnt, farms destroyed in, Mangu By Golok Nanmwa, JOS It was another night of fear in Mangu Local Government Area of Plateau State.As residents of Bin-Per community in Kombun District went to sleep on Monday night, August 17, few could have imagined that heavily armed attackers were already closing in on their homes. By about 11:30pm and into the early hours of Tuesday, August 18, the community was plunged into terror as gunmen reportedly opened fire on local vigilantes before splitting into groups and moving from house to house. By the time the attackers withdrew, at least 24 persons had been killed, according to community sources, while others sustained injuries. Several homes were reportedly burnt and farmlands and crops destroyed, leaving families devastated and a community struggling to comprehend the scale of the tragedy. The victims were later given a mass burial. But beyond the figures, the horror of Bin-Per was captured in the stories of survivors who watched loved ones disappear in the darkness. For many residents, the most painful part was that the attacks took place inside homes, where families had sought refuge from the violence and expected to be safe. An eyewitness, Daniel Musa, said the attackers moved from house to house, forcing their way into homes and attacking residents who were asleep. “Our village came under attack in the early hours of today, Tuesday, by heavily armed persons. “They were moving from house to house, opening the doors of people who were sleeping and slaughtering them,” he said. Eight family members killed The extent of the carnage became even more disturbing as residents recounted how entire families were wiped out. A resident, Mr Fangwsak James, said eight members of one family were killed in a compound, leaving behind only a two-year-old child who survived the attack despite sustaining gunshot wounds to the leg and hip. James said the child was left for dead before being discovered. Another resident, Shedrack Ayuba, said he lost his wife and four children in the attack. According to Ayuba, he was keeping watch over the community with other vigilantes when they suddenly heard gunshots from different directions. “I was with some of my co-vigilantes keeping watch over the community when we heard shooting from all over,” he said. Ayuba said he attempted to escape through a building but was shot in the leg. “I managed to escape through a maize farm. My wife and children were not spared. “They went into my house and opened fire on them while they were sleeping. “I was taken to the hospital. It was the next day that I discovered that my wife had been killed,” he said. Another resident said a man lost three children in the attack, further highlighting the devastating impact of the violence on families. Residents said the attackers appeared to have carefully positioned themselves around the community to prevent people from escaping. “They positioned themselves strategically and scattered themselves so that nobody would escape,” one resident said, adding that some people attempting to flee were also attacked and killed. “They did not spare anyone. They killed everyone,” another resident, Tongret Rogo, said. Vigilantes overrun Ronbak Maxwell, another resident, said the attackers first opened fire on vigilantes before gaining access to the community. He said the incident started at about 11:30pm and that about two vigilantes were killed before the attackers advanced into the community. According to him, the gunmen divided themselves into groups and began moving from house to house. “We called for help but the response was not fast,” Maxwell said. He added that most of the casualties were women and children. The attack also destroyed the economic foundation of many households. Women protest killings As the community buried its dead, women of Bin-Per took their grief to the streets. Carrying leaves, the women staged a peaceful protest against the killings and demanded urgent action from the government. They lamented the loss of husbands, children, relatives, neighbours and friends, saying the attack had left families traumatised and livelihoods devastated. One of the protesters, Mrs Ladi Joshua, said the women were devastated by the killings and demanded an end to recurring attacks on the community. “The scale of destruction is not merely an attack on individuals but an attack on an entire community, its dignity, livelihood, and future,” the women said. They questioned how heavily armed attackers could repeatedly penetrate vulnerable communities and inflict such destruction. The women also expressed concern over the effectiveness and responsiveness of the existing security architecture, saying communities were increasingly being forced to rely on themselves for protection. According to them, the intervention of youths helped prevent the death toll from becoming even higher. “Citizens should not have to become their own soldiers before they can sleep safely in their homes,” they said. However, they stressed that community self-defence could not replace the responsibility of government to protect lives and property. They called on Governor Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang and the Federal Government to urgently reassess security arrangements in vulnerable communities. They demanded improved intelligence gathering, proactive deployment of security personnel and effective rapid-response mechanisms. Assembly raises alarm The Plateau State House of Assembly has also raised concerns over the attack and its wider implications. During plenary, the member representing Mangu South Constituency, Dr Matthew Sylvester Kwarpo, raised a Matter of Urgent Public Importance over the attacks. Kwarpo said more than 25 people were killed in Bin-Per, while another person was killed in attacks on Jwak and Murish communities. He disclosed that 38 houses were burnt, while several hectares of farmlands, barns containing stored grains and other valuables were destroyed. The lawmaker warned that the destruction of farms and stored food could worsen the hardship facing residents and threaten food security. He urged the Assembly to convene a critical stakeholders’ meeting to examine the implications of the attacks on affected communities and Mangu Local Government Area. Kwarpo also called for proactive security measures, stronger intelligence gathering, improved surveillance and timely deployment of security personnel to vulnerable locations. He appealed to the Plateau State Government, State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, humanitarian agencies and well-meaning individuals to provide relief materials, food, medical assistance and shelter to victims. Governor orders intensified security Following the attack, Governor Mutfwang directed security agencies to intensify surveillance and patrols in Bin-Per, Kombun District and other vulnerable communities in Mangu. The state government condemned the attack and described it as a disturbing development capable of threatening the peace and security being consolidated across the state. The governor sympathised with the victims and their families and urged residents not to embark on reprisal attacks. He also called on residents to provide credible and timely information to security agencies to assist in identifying and apprehending the attackers. Police vow arrests The Plateau State Police Command has also moved to reassure residents. The Commissioner of Police, CP Ayodeji Faniyan, visited Bin-Per for an on-the-spot assessment of the situation. Faniyan commiserated with traditional council elders, the local government chairman and residents of Mangu and delivered the condolence message of the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu. The CP vowed that the perpetrators would be identified, arrested and prosecuted. “The Command will do everything within its constitutional powers to identify, arrest and prosecute those responsible,” he said. Faniyan said security had been strengthened in Bin-Per and surrounding communities to prevent further attacks and restore confidence among residents. He urged residents to provide accurate and timely information that could assist the investigation. He also warned against jungle justice, saying taking the law into their own hands could further escalate tension and undermine efforts to bring the perpetrators to justice. Attack rekindles old fears The Bin-Per attack did not occur in isolation. It came barely days after gunmen reportedly attacked Juwak Mai Tunbi community in Mangu, where properties, including tin sheds, places of worship and a chemist, were reportedly destroyed. The latest violence has therefore revived concerns over the vulnerability of communities in Mangu and the wider security situation in Plateau State. The attack has also attracted condemnation from political actors. A scribe of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, in Plateau State, Hon. Jude Eli Dakur, described the killings as “barbaric, senseless and unacceptable.” Dakur mourned the loss of innocent lives and condemned the destruction of homes, farms and property. He said the killing of people who were asleep in their homes represented a grave assault on the sanctity of human life. He called on security agencies to immediately mobilise and go after the perpetrators, while demanding intensified intelligence gathering and surveillance across Mangu and other vulnerable parts of Plateau State. He also called for effective rapid-response mechanisms capable of responding promptly to distress calls. The Plateau Initiative for Development and Advancement of the Natives, PIDAN, Central Zone, has called on the Plateau State Government to declare a state of emergency on security following the killing of more than 20 persons in Mangu Local Government Area. PIDAN made the demand while reacting to the latest attack on Binper community in Mangu, where more than 20 persons were reportedly killed and buried on Tuesday. In a strongly worded statement signed by its Chairman, Central Zone, Alpha John Dakwak and made available to newsmen on Wednesday , the group said the recurring attacks across Plateau had become intolerable and demanded urgent, decisive measures to protect vulnerable communities. PIDAN said the latest massacre, coming amid a series of deadly attacks in the state, demonstrated that government could no longer afford to respond to killings with condolences and condemnations alone. “Condolences are no substitute for security. Expressions of grief cannot resurrect the dead. What the people need now is decisive action, not another cycle of condemnation and condolences,” the group said. It declared: “Enough is enough,” insisting that the magnitude of the security crisis required “extraordinary, immediate and unequivocal action.” The group specifically urged the Plateau Government to declare a state of emergency on security in affected and vulnerable communities and take all necessary measures to protect lives and property. PIDAN also called for the equipping, training and proper coordination of local vigilantes to complement conventional security agencies, particularly in remote communities. The organisation further demanded a review of the current deployment of military personnel in communities. It called on the National Assembly to urgently fast-track the passage of the State Police Bill, saying the move would strengthen community-based policing and improve security across the country. PIDAN further urged security agencies to become more proactive through improved intelligence gathering, early-warning systems and rapid-response mechanisms capable of preventing attacks before they occur. “The people of Plateau State deserve to live in peace, farm their lands and raise their families without the constant fear of being attacked,” the group said. While expressing solidarity with the victims, their families and affected communities, PIDAN demanded accountability and decisive action from government. “This is no longer a time for condemnation alone. It is a time for action the group declared. The post ‘Gunmen went from house to house, killing people who were sleeping’ – Survivors of Plateau night of horror appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Reading Thucydides in the wolf world
items.description: The term Thucydides’s Trap has caught on since Professor Graham Allison wrote his 2017 book, Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap? The core concept comes from Greek soldier-historian Thucydides’s History of the Peloponnesian War who identifies the structural stress that occurs when a major rising power is perceived to threaten to displace an established power. My intention here is not to explain Allison’s work or his treatment of the trap but to point to how modern-day scholars and policymakers cherrypick episodes from Thucydides’s work to justify their own approaches. I believe, as the post-World War II international security architecture unravels and we enter what some describe as the wolf world, that it is important to analyse Thucydides’s history in view of the book’s hermeneutics rather than picking up episodes that suit one’s own predilections. Thucydides arrived in the United States policy corridors with Dr Henry Kissinger. He had taught the text at Harvard and was keenly familiar with it. But upon joining Richard Nixon’s administration in the White House, he sought fit to focus on the Melian Dialogue, colouring outside the lines. The one line, “The strong exact what they can; the weak concede what they must,” became the slogan of Cold War strategies. Kissinger knew that Thucydides message was far more nuanced and he was not justifying imperial overreach. But that was for the classroom. The world Kissinger had to tackle was one in which ‘man was wolf to man,’ homo homini lupus of Plautus popularised by Thomas Hobbes. That misrepresentation has generally informed US policymakers since then. Now that cruder minds are ruling America and the precepts of International Law, for whatever they were worth, have been defenestrated and America’s foreign policy has become a Kabuki theatre, a few words about Thucydides’s work are in order. The structural architecture of History of the Peloponnesian War relies on a psychological arc that connects the Plague of Athens, the Melian Dialogue (nearly 14 years later) and the Sicilian Expedition (a year later). Far from putting down a simple chronicle of military manoeuvres, Thucydides tracks the internal rot of the Athenian psyche through the description of the Plague. By tracing this trajectory, the reader discovers that the moral dissolution initiated by the plague directly fostered the intellectual hubris that were to lead to Melos, which inevitably culminated in the material ruin of the Sicilian campaign. The foundational fracture occurs in Book Two with the Plague (430 BCE). Thucydides describes a city where the sudden, indiscriminate terror of death obliterates law ( nomos ) and religious restraint. Faced with immediate mortality, citizens abandon honour for instant gratification, arguing that the virtuous and the wicked die alike. This lawlessness ( anomia ) institutionalises a new societal ethos: the abandonment of traditional justice in favour of self-interest and survival. The plague does not merely kill bodies; it extinguishes the moral constraints of the polis. Might and appetite replace civic virtue. The plague, Thucydides tells us, also claimed Pericles and his family. That death, within the hermeneutics of the text, becomes a metaphor for the demise of nomos. The emergence of more populist and aggressive figures, such as Cleon, who prioritised personal popularity and raw emotion over steady strategy, comes to symbolise anomia. This internalised lawlessness manifests later as aggressive foreign policy in the Melian Dialogue (416 BCE) of Book Five. But the seeds of Melos were sown earlier. Two years after Pericles’ death, Athens had the Mytilenian debate between Cleon and Diodotus. Cleon fiercely argued in favour of executing the entire population of Mytilene to send a message of terror. While Diodotus narrowly persuaded the assembly to reverse the decision to execute all citizens, the Athenians still exacted a brutal and bloody punishment on the city. At Melos, the Athenian envoys articulate a chilling political realism, famously declaring that, “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” This worldview seems to be the direct philosophical descendant of the plague’s nihilism. Having lost their respect for divine law and cosmic justice during the pestilence, the Athenians now claim that the rule of the stronger is a universal law of nature. The moral decay hardened into intellectual hubris. Athens no longer seeks to justify its empire through justice or leadership, but purely through raw, unyielding power. The immediate narrative pivot to the Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) in Book Six reveals this hubris in action, dramatised through the opposing speeches of Nicias and Alcibiades. Nicias represents the ghost of old Athenian moderation. He desperately warns the assembly against overreach, cautioning that they are leaving enemies behind to chase a massive, unknown island. But the plague-damaged psyche of Athens, now driven entirely by imperial appetite and the illusion of invincibility, cannot tolerate restraint. Instead, they rally behind Alcibiades (notice the shift from the Cleon-Diodotus debate). Alcibiades is brilliant, reckless, and entirely devoid of civic responsibility. He appeals to the city’s insatiable desire for expansion, arguing that an empire must grow or it will wither. Ultimately, Thucydides’s narrative acts as a tragic warning. The lawlessness born in the plague pits became the strategic blindness that was to mock the Melians and finally drove Athens to sail into the Sicilian trap. In Sicily, the inversion is completed. The Athenians are utterly destroyed, reduced to the same desperate reliance on “hope” and suffering that they had ridiculed at Melos. Through this connection Thucydides demonstrates that the real danger of power overreach is not always external opposition but the internal erosion of the moral and intellectual clarity required to understand the limits of power. There are no perfect analogies but history’s verdicts are often uncannily similar. Header image: An AI-generated bust of Henry Kissinger in the likeness of Thucydides.

items.title: 2027: Obi lists five critical questions that should shape polls, begins campaign in Onitsha
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu & Henry Umoru TWO days after the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, removed the lid, 2027 Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Mr Peter Obi, yesterday, commenced campaigns in Onitsha, his homeland in Anambra State, in style. Read Also: Governor Adeleke’s victory: Nigerians must replicate Osun experience in 2027 — Lawyers, activists Obi, who said Nigeria can work and must work, unveiled his agenda in critical sectors and listed five critical questions that should inform the choice of voters in the election. “Are Nigerians better off than they were four years ago? Can they afford food, education, and healthcare? Can businesses produce, expand, and create jobs? Can young people find productive work? Can farmers work safely and get their produce to market?These are the measures that matter” he said. Addressing newsmen at his Onitsha residence to mark the commencement of his campaign, Obi promised that he and his running mate, Dr Rabiu Kwankwaso will defeat insecurity, pull people out of poverty, drastically reduce hunger and the number of out-of-school children, as well as improve education and healthcare and build growth that serves everyone, especially the most vulnerable. He said that as the campaigns begin, all candidates for the election must be willing to present their credentials, defend their records, and subject their vision to open scrutiny. “No candidate should hide behind the high walls of power, send proxies or surrogates to the hustings, and expect Nigerians to entrust them with the leadership of the country. “Every candidate seeking the presidency must have the courage to come before the people, answer their questions, defend their records, and subject their vision to public scrutiny. “True leadership requires presence and empathy. No one can lead from the front without standing with communities across Nigeria devastated by banditry, criminality, terrorism, and flooding. You cannot truly lead people you are unwilling to visit, listen to, and understand”, he said. He expressed clear commitment that he and his running mate will take their message directly to Nigerians. “We will listen to them, understand their concerns, and engage them openly. We will not delegate this duty to proxies. We will answer questions, defend our record and character, and present our plan to rebuild Nigeria. “Any presidential candidate who lacks the resolve to travel across the country, meet the people, and respond to their questions lacks the capacity to govern it”, he added. Obi said further: “I commit to commencing the journey of resetting Nigeria by uniting it, securing it on the path of economic and inclusive growth, and moving our country from consumption to production. “The campaign period gives every citizen an opportunity to join the national conversation. I urge Nigerians to examine each candidate’s record and proposals, ask tough questions, and demand evidence behind every promise. “We should debate ideas without hatred, compete without violence, and disagree without weakening the bonds that unite us. When Nigerians make their choice, that choice must be respected. “Democracy does not end on election day. Citizens must continue to demand transparency, accountability, and results from those entrusted with the mandate to govern. “Nigeria’s challenges are real, but so are its opportunities. We have the people, resources, enterprise, and creativity to build a safer, more productive country. Our task is to turn these possibilities into results. We have the credentials, experience, and record to collaborate with Nigerians on this transformative journey. “Our journey will be harder if we do not unite as one people and one nation. A united Nigeria, guided by shared purpose and a commitment to fairness, justice, and equity, will make transformation easier, strengthen our institutions, and help us hold our leaders accountable. “The 2027 election must be guided by capacity, competence, compassion, character, and commitment. Our campaign will focus on the urgent concerns of Nigerians and not on ethnicity or religion. Nigerians must reject and disregard any campaign driven by propaganda, ethnicity, religion, elitism, or cronyism. “As my team and I travel across the country, we will listen to Nigerians, understand their needs and concerns, and assure them that we have the competence, character, and compassion to lead and reset Nigeria for the benefit of all.” On the state of the nation, Obi said sustainable development requires more than reactive reform, adding that reform is not the goal, but that better lives are. According to him, the World Bank’s April 2026 Nigeria development update made it clear that Nigeria’s challenge is how to turn economic reform and stabilisation into improved livelihoods, stronger human capital, wider opportunities, and inclusive growth. “We will pursue practical reforms that deliver lasting results, combining fiscal discipline with productive investment, as Senator Kwankwaso and I have demonstrated. The post 2027: Obi lists five critical questions that should shape polls, begins campaign in Onitsha appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: JoyNews-Republic Bank Habitat Fair: Day 2 opens today with bigger homeownership opportunities
items.description: Prospective homeowners, property investors, developers and construction enthusiasts are expected to converge on the Achimota Mall today, Saturday, August 22, 2026, as the JoyNews-Republic Bank Habitat Fair 2026 mini-fair enters its second day. Following an encouraging opening day that attracted visitors eager to explore opportunities in Ghana’s housing and construction sector, organisers are preparing for another full day of exhibitions, expert engagements and opportunities for patrons to connect directly with businesses shaping the housing market. The three-day mini-fair, which runs from Friday, August 21 to Sunday, August 23, is being held under the theme “Dream it. Explore it. Own it.” More to explore on Day 2 Day Two is expected to provide patrons with another opportunity to engage exhibitors and explore solutions spanning home ownership, property investment, construction, building materials, home improvement and related services. Visitors can interact directly with participating businesses, ask questions, compare available options and seek practical guidance as they plan their next steps towards acquiring, building or improving a home. For prospective homeowners, the fair offers an opportunity to move beyond simply dreaming about owning a house to exploring the products, services and professional support needed to make that ambition achievable. Property investors and industry professionals can also use the platform to engage businesses and explore opportunities across Ghana’s housing ecosystem. A weekend of housing opportunities The strong turnout on Friday has set the pace for what promises to be an engaging weekend at the Achimota Mall, with organisers encouraging members of the public who missed Day One to make Saturday an opportunity to discover what the fair has to offer. The event will be open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. today and tomorrow, Sunday, August 23. The mini-fair is being organised in partnership with Republic Bank, under its brand promise “We’re the one for you!”, and powered by Drive EV GH, which promotes sustainable mobility. Other partners supporting the initiative are Virtual Security Africa, Akwaaba Building Materials, Lesh Fortune Ltd, MTN, Door Masters, Ayuda, Western Vilas, CTECHI Ghana LTD, Saint-Gobain Ghana, Sintex Tank, Interplast and Clifton Homes. Their participation brings together different components of the housing and construction value chain, giving patrons an opportunity to discover a broad range of products and services under one roof. Building towards the main Habitat Fair The mini-fair also serves as part of the activities leading up to the main Republic Bank JoyNews Habitat Fair 2026, which seeks to connect prospective homeowners with businesses and professionals within Ghana’s housing and property sector. The initiative is therefore positioning the weekend event not simply as an exhibition, but as a platform where ideas, expertise and opportunities can meet. For visitors, the message from organisers remains simple: “Get a house, make it a home.” With two days still available, patrons have the opportunity to visit the Achimota Mall, explore the exhibition stands, engage industry players and take practical steps towards turning their housing aspirations into reality.

items.title: Léon XIV à Saint-Marin : la diplomatie des micro-États, une stratégie vaticane ?
items.description: Aujourd’hui, samedi 22 août, Léon XIV effectue son cinquième voyage apostolique hors d’Italie dans la République de Saint-Marin, enclavée au cœur de la péninsule italienne. Le pape répond ainsi à l’invitation des deux capitaines-régents, Alice Mina et Vladimiro Selva, qui exercent conjointement les fonctions de chefs d’État de la République. La visite devrait être brève – la matinée pour Saint-Marin, l’après-midi pour la ville portuaire voisine de Rimini, en Italie – et le protocole simplifié, à l’instar de celui en usage pour les visites pastorales dans la péninsule. Arrivé en hélicoptère, il sera accueilli au Palazzo Publico, puis aura un entretien particulier avec les seuls capitaines-régents. Léon XIV prononcera un discours devant le Grand Conseil général, tout comme il l'avait déjà fait devant le Congrès espagnol, puis il saluera la foule depuis le balcon de l’Hôtel de Ville de Saint-Marin et lui donnera sa bénédiction apostolique. Viendra ensuite l’étape plus proprement religieuse du voyage, avec une adoration eucharistique dans la basilique éponyme, qui est également la co-cathédrale du diocèse de Saint-Marin-Montefeltro. L’après-midi, de retour en Italie, le pape rencontrera les religieuses augustines contemplatives de Pennabili, qui suivent la même règle que les religieux de Saint-Augustin, l’ordre dont il est issu. Ce monastère s’est signalé par son assistance aux déplacés et aux fugitifs durant la Seconde Guerre mondiale. À Rimini, où est organisée une « Rencontre pour l’amitié entre les peuples » par le mouvement de laïcs catholiques Communion et Libération, proche de la Démocratie chrétienne historique et très puissant en Italie du Nord, le pape visitera deux expositions : l’une consacrée à saint Augustin, dont on sait à quel point le pape s’est imprégné de la pensée ; une autre consacrée à Léon Harmel (1829-1915), laïc dévot proche de Léon XIII qui, aux côtés du député Albert de Mun, fait figure de modèle dans l’application de la doctrine sociale de l’Eglise par le patronat chrétien du Nord. Léon XIV achèvera la journée par une rencontre dans la cathédrale de Rimini avec des malades, organisée par Caritas Italie, puis par la célébration de la messe. Pourquoi le pape a-t-il décidé de se rendre dans cette minuscule République – le 5e État le plus petit et le moins peuplé au monde, avec 34 000 habitants pour 61 km² – qui fait figure de survivance des cités-États de l’Europe pré-westphalienne ? Il faut d’abord noter que Léon XIV n’est pas le premier pape de l’époque moderne à visiter Saint-Marin : Jean-Paul II (en 1982) puis Benoît XVI (en 2011) s’y sont également rendus. Le déplacement à Saint-Marin peut également être considéré comme un signe de la sollicitude pastorale dont les papes font preuve envers la péninsule italienne, une région où ils voyagent bien plus fréquemment que dans tout autre endroit. Mais il y a sans doute quelque chose de plus : Saint-Marin et l’État de la Cité du Vatican partagent en effet beaucoup de points communs. Tous deux font remonter leur fondation à l’Empire romain, au Ier siècle : pour le pouvoir pontifical, au martyre de saint Pierre sous Néron ; pour Saint-Marin, à l’établissement, dans une région montagneuse, d’une petite communauté chrétienne d’hommes libres réunis autour de Marinus, un diacre ermite et ancien tailleur de pierre venu de Dalmatie, mort martyr vers 366, et qui donne son nom à la République, pour fuir les persécutions de Dioclétien. Même si ce récit des origines est empreint de légendes, la République date son commencement officiel du 3 septembre 301 et revendique le titre d'État le plus ancien au monde ayant continuellement subsisté. Pour autant qu’on puisse le savoir, « l’indépendance » juridique de la cité de Saint-Marin est plutôt un fruit du mouvement communal italien des XIIe-XIIIe siècles. La devise de Saint-Marin, Libertas , revendique encore hautement cette tradition de franchises municipales. Il est en revanche indéniable que Saint-Marin constitue la plus ancienne République au monde, et également la République dont la Constitution, inchangée depuis 1600, est en vigueur depuis le plus longtemps – 426 ans. La République de Saint-Marin qui, comme Venise autrefois, revendique de se faire appeler « Sérénissime », apparaît à la fois comme un vestige de la vieille Europe et du poids de l’histoire, et comme un signe paradoxal de « modernité », ou plutôt d’intemporalité des valeurs démocratiques. Au XIXe siècle, les attitudes du Saint-Siège et de Saint-Marin à l’égard de l’unification italienne apparaissent presque diamétralement opposées. Alors que Pie IX, pourtant un temps pressenti à la tête d’une Confédération italienne, s’arc-boute sur la défense des États pontificaux et de son pouvoir temporel, Saint-Marin, dont l’indépendance avait déjà été respectée par Napoléon, offre en 1849 l’hospitalité à Garibaldi, pourchassé par les troupes pontificales. En reconnaissance, les partisans de l’unité italienne renoncent à toute velléité annexionniste sur la petite République, qui signe en 1862 une convention d’amitié préservatrice avec le nouveau royaume d’Italie, proclamé l’année précédente. Saint-Marin présente également la singularité d’avoir été le premier et le seul pays d’Europe occidentale où un gouvernement communiste a pu se mettre en place à la suite d’élections libres, et gouverner entre 1945 et 1957. À l’exception de la période fasciste, où la République s’est dotée d’un gouvernement qui partageait en apparence les orientations mussoliniennes afin d’éviter l’annexion, les gouvernements de gauche et du centre l’ont dominée durant tout le XXe siècle. L’intérêt de Léon XIV pour Saint-Marin découle également de leur situation commune de micro-États européens. Au Vatican, l’articulation des pouvoirs temporel et religieux est singulière, le rôle de chef de l’Église catholique offrant au pape un rayonnement mondial, inversement proportionnel à la taille de son État, qui ne vaut comme gage formel et support territorial de son indépendance totale. Mais pour leur fonctionnement courant, Saint-Marin et le Vatican sont tous deux dépendants de la République italienne, qui est la garante internationalement reconnue de leur indépendance – l’Italie est ainsi tenue d’assurer la défense du Vatican. Sans être formellement membres ni de l’Union ni de la zone euro, les deux micro-États sont autorisés à utiliser l’euro comme monnaie nationale. La population saint-marinaise n’est d’ailleurs pas hostile à l’idée d’intégration européenne, comme l’a montré en 2013 le résultat d’un référendum local sur l’adhésion (le oui l’avait emporté à 50,8 %). Mais la perspective d’une adhésion reste lointaine, d’autant plus que Saint-Marin jouit déjà de l’union douanière, de la libre circulation avec l’Italie, et de la plupart des avantages de l’Union sans en être membre. Comme le Vatican, Saint-Marin a une tradition diplomatique neutraliste, ce qui lui permet d’entretenir à son échelle de bonnes relations avec les États-Unis comme la Chine. Fidèle à sa tradition de défense de l’indépendance nationale face à un voisin plus puissant, la République a condamné fermement l’invasion russe de l’Ukraine. Pour le gouvernement italien, les relations avec le Vatican comme avec Saint-Marin sont regardées, sinon comme des affaires de politique intérieure, du moins comme des questions à propos desquelles l’Italie dispose d’un droit de regard particulier. Le nonce du Vatican en Italie, qui joue un rôle clef dans les nominations d’évêques, est également accrédité auprès de Saint-Marin, dont 6 000 habitants sont d’ailleurs citoyens italiens. On retrouve un fonctionnement analogue entre la France et Monaco, dont la République française se porte garante de l’indépendance, au prix d’un droit de regard sur les affaires intérieures de la principauté (elle intervient par exemple dans la nomination du ministre d’État, le chef du gouvernement monégasque). Il paraît naturel que ces micro-États renforcent entre eux leurs relations déjà bonnes, comme leur taille leur confronte à des questions de gouvernance similaires. À la différence de Monaco, Saint-Marin ne peut en aucun cas apparaître comme un paradis fiscal – la différence des prix avec l’Italie est contenue par de nombreux accords pour éviter la concurrence déloyale. Du point de vue du pape, le principal intérêt des micro-États européens pourrait résider aussi dans la place importante qu’y détient l’Église catholique. À Saint-Marin, contrairement à Malte, à Monaco, au Liechtenstein, et bien sûr au Vatican, le catholicisme n’est certes plus religion d’État, mais il représente encore la confession de plus de 90 % des habitants, en majorité pratiquants, et l’Église reste très présente dans la vie sociale. Pour le Saint-Siège, la situation de Saint-Marin représente sans doute un compromis enviable entre la défense de la liberté religieuse reconnue à tous les citoyens dans la constitution, et une empreinte de la religion catholique dans la vie sociale et culturelle, même si les lignes évoluent : en 2022, la légalisation de l’avortement a été votée par le Grand Conseil général. À Monaco, en revanche, le catholicisme demeure la seule religion officielle en vertu de la Constitution, et le prince Albert a récemment opposé son veto à une loi libéralisant l’accès à l’IVG. Au Liechtenstein, le prince a menacé de faire de même en cas de légalisation de l’avortement par référendum ou par le Parlement. En Andorre, où la Constitution reconnaît une collaboration particulière des pouvoirs publics avec l'Église catholique – sans toutefois faire d'elle une Église nationale –, des tensions sur le même sujet opposent le gouvernement andorran au Saint-Siège. L'un des deux co-princes, chefs de l'État andorran aux côtés du président de la République française, est en effet statutairement un ecclésiastique : l'évêque d'Urgel, en Espagne. Sur ce dossier, celui-ci s'est montré plus ouvert que la Curie romaine à des négociations avec le gouvernement andorran. Malte présente une configuration particulière : le plus grand des micro-États du continent est aussi le seul membre de l’Union, le catholicisme y est toujours religion d’État, et l’avortement y demeure très restreint malgré le cadre plus contraignant des traités européens. Du reste, l’intérêt des papes modernes pour Malte est également très vif : Jean-Paul II (1990 puis 2001), Benoît XVI (2010) et François (2022) s’y sont rendus, et il serait surprenant que Léon XIV, qui a montré son appétence pour les voyages apostoliques, n’y aille pas également. Les gestes du Saint-Siège en direction des micro-États européens (comme des autres petits États, ainsi que certaines îles du Pacifique comme Nauru et Tuvalu, qui devenues emblématiques de la lutte contre le réchauffement climatique) seront donc à scruter de près au cours des prochains mois. D’une certaine manière, cet intérêt diplomatique prolonge en le réorientant le souci pastoral de François en direction des « périphéries », même si le pape argentin privilégiait les pays plus éloignés, où la situation de l’Église était des plus précaires, ce qui n’est plus le cas ici. Progressivement, Léon XIV semble tracer les contours d'une véritable stratégie diplomatique en direction des micro-États. Au-delà des problématiques communes que ces États partagent, l'intérêt du pape pour ces espaces interstitiels de la mondialisation montre qu'à l'ère des prédateurs, il existe encore des stratégies d'influence et de visibilité qui ne passent pas par l'affirmation de la puissance brute. Dans cette configuration, Saint-Marin ne constitue pas seulement le micro-État qui partage le plus de traits culturels communs avec le Vatican. Sans nier les tensions qu'amène l'exercice de toute vie démocratique pluraliste, la République représente aussi, aux yeux du Saint-Siège, un exemple d'équilibre entre tradition et modernité – entre intégration des valeurs européennes, d'une part, et avantages d'une marginalité volontaire, de l'autre. C'est cette logique d'accompagnement plutôt que d'adhésion pleine et entière que le Saint-Siège entend précisément faire sienne au sein des instances européennes et internationales. Si Saint-Marin a survécu à Napoléon et Garibaldi, alors le Vatican peut bien résister à Trump, et prendre tout son temps pour cela : leur permanence, au milieu du champ de ruines de l’histoire européenne, est en elle-même un démenti constant et cinglant aux logiques de la puissance brute. L’article Léon XIV à Saint-Marin : la diplomatie des micro-États, une stratégie vaticane ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: ‘Africa’s prosperity is not a threat to anybody’ — Mahama
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has rejected concerns that a more prosperous and self-reliant Africa could pose a threat to the rest of the world, saying the continent’s economic advancement would instead contribute to global prosperity. He said Africa must now move beyond the political liberation struggles championed by its founding leaders and confront what he described as the economic struggle confronting the current generation. President Mahama made the remarks in an interview with TRT World on Friday, August 21, 2026, during which he called for a fundamental shift in Africa’s engagement with the international community. ‘Not a threat to anybody’ President Mahama was emphatic that Africa’s pursuit of economic prosperity should not be viewed as a zero-sum proposition in which the continent’s gains would come at the expense of other regions. “Africa’s prosperity is not a threat to anybody,” he said. He suggested that the economic transformation of African countries would have wider benefits, creating stronger markets and new opportunities while enabling the continent to address longstanding challenges. His comments come amid growing calls across Africa for greater economic self-reliance, increased local value addition and stronger African participation in decisions concerning the continent’s resources and development. For President Mahama, the next chapter of Africa’s transformation is, therefore, not simply about political independence but about acquiring the economic strength and negotiating power necessary to determine the continent’s place in the global order. Partnerships, not dependency President Mahama stressed that his call for greater African self-reliance should not be interpreted as a rejection of international cooperation. Rather, he said, Africa should engage its international partners from a position that gives it greater influence over the terms of cooperation and the use of its resources. “We don’t reject partnerships, but those partnerships must be on our terms,” he said. For the president, the objective is to build an Africa that can determine its own development priorities while continuing to engage constructively with the global community. He said a stronger African voice would enable the continent to participate more effectively in decisions shaping the global economy and its own future. “Africa cannot continue to be a dependent continent. There are things we can do so that we are able to have a better voice in global affairs,” he said. From political to economic liberation According to President Mahama, the priorities confronting African leaders today are different from those faced by the continent’s independence-era leaders. He cited Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, and other African leaders who led the struggle for political independence, saying the continent had now entered another phase of its development. “The challenge that us leaders of Africa today face is not the liberation struggle that was fought by Kwame Nkrumah and our forebears. It is the economic struggle,” he said. He argued that African countries must therefore strengthen their economies, increase their influence in international affairs and reduce their dependence on external support.

items.title: Maryam fires a fresh salvo at PPP, PTI
items.description: LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz on Friday fired a fresh salvo at coalition partner Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), accusing it of corruption and warning political rivals against targeting her government’s performance. “One party (PPP) is involved in corruption and the other (PTI) in anarchy. I would like to ask them to follow in the footsteps of the PML-N to serve the people,” Maryam said while speaking at the inauguration of a cardiac transplant centre at the Jinnah Institute of Cardiology here on Friday. The chief minister’s remarks appear to signal a hardening of PML-N’s stance towards the PPP, which has recently intensified its criticism of the federal and Punjab governments over their political mandate and alleged electoral irregularities in Azad Kashmir. The latest exchange has exposed growing strains within the ruling alliance, with PPP leaders repeatedly describing the PML-N governments as products of a “Form-47 mandate”, while PML-N leaders have increasingly hit back by questioning the PPP’s record of governance. Ms Nawaz’s cabinet members, particularly Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, have already been engaged in a war of words with the PPP, mainly over the latter’s criticism of the Punjab government’s performance and its references to Form-47 following the Kashmir elections. On Friday, CM Maryam herself entered the fray, making it clear that her government would respond if the PPP continued to target the PML-N, particularly over its governance in Punjab. Earlier, Ms Bokhari had accused the PPP of being unable to “digest” the pace of development in Punjab under Ms Maryam’s administration. “Those who are envious of Punjab’s progress and prosperity may continue to criticise, but the journey of public service will not stop,” Bokhari had said. The PPP, however, has maintained that the PML-N lacks the moral authority to question its governance or political standing. Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon recently accused the PML-N of having come to power on the basis of a “ fake mandate ”. “The public knows who came to power through Form-47 and who enjoys the real mandate. The PML-N has been pursuing politics marked by arrogance, intolerance and provocative rhetoric,” he said. The PPP’s criticism echoes a central allegation made by Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) since the Feb 8, 2024 general elections — that the election results were manipulated to deprive the party of seats and facilitate the formation of PML-N-led governments. The increasingly sharp rhetoric between the two coalition partners comes despite their continued political cooperation at the federal level. The exchanges suggest that while the two parties remain allies in government, their political interests — particularly in Punjab and Sindh — are becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile. Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

When the Belly Begins to Speak: The Beautiful Mystery of Pregnancy’s Dark Mark
items.description: One day, you look at your growing belly and notice something you may never have seen before: a faint line running down the middle of your abdomen. A few weeks later, it is darker. Then the questions begin. Is this normal? Does it mean I’m having a boy? Is my baby taking all my melanin? Will the line disappear after delivery? For many expectant mothers, the appearance of this dark line can be surprising, especially for women who have never experienced it before. But that mysterious pregnancy mark has a name: linea nigra. And while social media is full of theories about what it means, the science behind it is much less dramatic and actually quite fascinating. From a Faint Line to a Dark Pregnancy Mark Before pregnancy, most women already have a faint vertical line running down the abdomen. It is called the linea alba, which means “white line.” It is usually barely noticeable because it has little pigmentation. During pregnancy, however, hormonal changes can stimulate the skin’s pigment-producing cells, known as melanocytes. As melanin production increases, the previously faint linea alba can become darker and more visible. That is when it becomes known as the linea nigra, or “black line.” The line may run from the belly button down towards the pubic area. In some women, it can extend upwards towards the chest. And no two women necessarily experience it in the same way. For some, it is barely visible. For others, it can become quite dark and prominent. So, Why Does Pregnancy Make the Skin Darker? Pregnancy brings a major hormonal shift. Levels of hormones such as estrogen and progesterone rise, and these changes can influence melanin production and distribution in the skin. That is also why some pregnant women notice darker nipples, darker patches on the face or other areas of increased pigmentation. So when someone says, “You’ve become darker because you’re pregnant,” there is a little truth behind the observation, but it is not because the baby is somehow “taking” or “needing” the mother’s melanin. Rather, pregnancy hormones can stimulate melanocytes, resulting in increased pigmentation. Does the Dark Line Mean the Baby Is a Boy or a Girl? Now, this is where things get interesting. For generations, people have had their own theories about the linea nigra. One popular belief says that if the line stops at the belly button, the baby is a girl. If it continues above the belly button towards the chest, the baby is supposedly a boy. Sounds convincing, right? Not quite. There is no scientific evidence that the length, darkness or appearance of the linea nigra can predict a baby’s sex. So if someone confidently looks at your belly and announces, “Definitely a boy!” based on the line, you may want to smile but wait for the medical confirmation. Is the Line a Sign That Something Is Wrong? For most pregnant women, no. The linea nigra is generally a normal and harmless consequence of pregnancy-related pigmentation changes. It does not usually cause pain or require treatment. It can become more noticeable as pregnancy progresses, particularly around the second trimester and beyond. And for many women, it gradually fades after childbirth as hormone levels return towards their pre-pregnancy state. The timing varies from person to person. Can You Stop It From Appearing? Not really. The linea nigra is a natural pregnancy change, so there is no guaranteed way to prevent it. However, increased exposure to sunlight can make pigmentation more noticeable, so protecting the skin from excessive sun exposure may help prevent it from becoming darker. Most importantly, there is no need to scrub, bleach or use harsh products in an attempt to remove it. Your belly is not dirty. It is simply responding to the remarkable changes happening inside your body. ‘My Body Is Drawing a Line for the Baby’ Some of the conversations around pregnancy pigmentation are rooted in curiosity, cultural beliefs and personal experiences. Women often share stories about suddenly noticing changes in their skin, sometimes wondering whether the changes are connected to their baby’s development. One popular social media explanation even suggests that the body is “preparing for life” by producing more melanin. While that makes for an interesting way of describing the experience, the scientific explanation is simpler: pregnancy hormones influence melanocytes, leading to increased pigmentation in certain areas of the skin. The body is certainly preparing for new life, but the dark line itself is not a biological signal telling the body to “create life.” More Than Just a Line Pregnancy can transform a woman’s body in ways she may never have anticipated. The belly grows. The breasts change. The skin may stretch and darken. Veins can become more visible. Hair and nails may change. And suddenly, a line that was almost invisible for years becomes one of the most noticeable features on the stomach. For some mothers, it may feel strange at first. For others, it becomes a beautiful reminder of the journey to motherhood. And yes, sometimes it becomes a conversation starter. “What’s that line?” “Is it a boy?” “Does it mean something?” The answer is simple: it is called the linea nigra, and in most cases, it is just one of the many normal changes that can accompany pregnancy. So, dear mama, if you look down and see that dark line stretching across your beautiful bump, don’t panic. It is not a curse. It is not a warning sign. And it certainly cannot tell you whether you are carrying a boy or a girl. It is simply your skin responding to the extraordinary hormonal journey of pregnancy. And when the baby finally arrives, that once-dark line will slowly begin to fade, leaving behind more than just a disappearing mark — a beautiful reminder of the incredible journey your body took to bring new life into the world.

items.title: ‘The Big Push is pushing’ – Upper West MPs hail contractors delivering in the region
items.description: “The Big Push is pushing.” That was the verdict as the Upper West Parliamentary Caucus inspected roads under President John Dramani Mahama’s flagship infrastructure agenda on Thursday, August 20. Their message after a day on the ground: Praise for contractors who are delivering, pressure for those behind schedule, and a promise from the contractor that work will be done by 2028. Leading the team, Caucus Leader Dr. Sebastian Sandaare said the visit to the Mwankuri-Han and the Han-Nandawwaala-Kuntulo- Jeffisi-Tumu portions was to verify work on the ground. The project has been awarded to five contractors. “These are roads under His Excellency John Dramani Mahama that have been awarded under the Big Push. We are here to see for ourselves what is happening. After this, we will report our observations to the Minister of Roads,” he said. “What we want is for the roads to be done on time and to be of good quality. You know how we struggle and how bad our roads are. Our people are crying for quality work, and the work should also be completed on time. P&W Ghanem Limited received the flowers and special praise. Lawra MP Bede A. Ziedeng commended the contractor for “neat” and “fast” work. “Those who cannot do the work, let’s take the contract from them and give to people who can do it. Without this road, Upper West will continue to suffer,” Nadowli-Kaleo MP Anthony Sumah Mwinkaara was specific. “He has done the prime on one side and is just two kilometres away from putting the second seal. The entire stretch here has the second seal done. At the rate he is going, he is the only one we are sure will finish before time.” Wa West MP, Supt. Retired Peter Lanchene Toobu wrapped up the caucus remarks. “P&W Ghanem is showing class. He’s showing speed. He’s showing competence. If all the contractors were working like this, I am quite convinced nobody in the region would be raising issues about delays. So far, so very good.” “We have told them that some of them are behind schedule, and we expect them to speed up, to double up. Briefing the MPs, Caesar Ghanem, the CEO of P&W Ghanem, explained the scope. “The first project runs from Manco Reef and it is 22 kilometers. So far we have completed the prime seal. We are currently doing the first seal, and we still have to do the second seal. In total it will be three layers,” he said. He said the second project covers 25 kilometers: 15km from Nandom towards Lawra and 10km from Nandom towards Lambussie. “So far we have completed the fill formation. Currently we are preparing for the sub-base. Hopefully next week we will start that layer, then the base, and then the seal work.” On timelines, he was confident. “The project is expected to be completed before the deadline, which is January or February 2028. Each project has a duration of two years. As you can see, the first project has been sealed almost entirely. The remaining work will not take much time.” He added that the overlay of asphalt promised by the Roads Minister will come under a separate contract. “For now, this contract covers three layers of surface dressing: prime seal and first seal.” The caucus also visited the site of Greenhouse limited at the Kuntulo stretch heading to Jeffisi to see the progress of work. Lawra MP, Bede Ziedeng also commented on P&W Ghanem’s work on the Han-Domini-Lawra Road, where sub-base works are complete. For road users, the impact is already real. Mr Hudu Nafa says his trip from Wa to Tumuh has been transformed. “I used to take four to five hours. But now, I’ve only used one hour and twenty minutes. The road is very nice.” “Let’s give thanks and praises, and we’ll continue to vote for the government. We are only appealing that they should continue with the rest of the road. From Kanyininguase to Wa is the only place that is not good for us now.” Nurudin Saani of the NHIA agreed. “Previously the road was very terrible. You could use almost four hours to Wa. Now I used two hours. When JM was saying it, a lot of people had doubts. But it has really come to reality.” Nadowli-Kaleo MP Anthony Sumah raised concerns about deteriorating sections. “From Magazine down to Jang, it is so bad. This is a place that was tarred initially, but it has gone very bad. We cannot be building new roads and neglecting the old ones that need maintenance. If the contractor does not come on site, we will meet with the Minister and suggest decisive action,” he said.

items.title: Dynamics of reorganisation
items.description: WHILE debating the question of carving out more ‘administrative units’ from Pakistan’s existing four provinces, we may find it relevant to study how India has reorganised its states (equivalent to our provinces) since independence. The example is pertinent because of the shared circumstances of the two countries created out of undivided India. They inherited the same interim constitution — the Government of India Act, 1935 — which each adapted to fit its own context. Both countries chose a parliamentary form of government. Pakistan adopted a more explicit federal character, while India shied away from calling itself a federation. Instead, it opted to describe itself as a ‘union with some federal characteristics’. Probably, India’s more diluted form of federalism helped it carve an uncomplicated path for creating new provinces: a simple majority in parliament and a non-binding consultation with the concerned states. On the other hand, Pakistan’s 1973 Constitution made the creation of new provinces contingent upon the passage of a resolution in the concerned provincial assembly or assemblies by a two-thirds majority before the bill for new provinces could be tabled in parliament and passed in the two Houses by a two-thirds majority. This set the bar very high for altering the boundaries of the provinces as compared to India. Around the time of Partition, undivided India consisted of 14 provinces and 587 princely states, of which two provinces (Bengal and Punjab) were partitioned. Both India and Pakistan received a part of each province. Three provinces — Sindh, the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and British Balochistan — joined Pakistan, taking the tally of provinces in India and Pakistan to 11 and five respectively. Thirteen princely states acceded to Pakistan. The rest either voluntarily acceded to India or were coerced into doing so through brute military force. Kashmir has remained a disputed territory ever since. The reorganisation of Indian states was triggered by language riots after a political activist, who had been demanding a separate state from Madras for Telugu-speaking people, died in 1952 following a fast unto death. When the riots spread, the Government of India fast-tracked the creation of the Telugu-speaking Andhra state (later called Andhra Pradesh) out of Madras state. The demands for more states based on language spread. The Indian government constituted a three-member States Reorganisation Commission in December 1953, headed by a former judge of the supreme court. As Pakistan debates new provinces, India’s experience offers relevant insights. The commission, constituted to propose the redrawing of state boundaries, also came to be known as the Justice Fazal Ali Commission after the chairman. Its proceedings continued for about 21 months and it submitted its report in September 1955. Parliament finally passed the States Reorganisation Act in 1956, leading to the redrawing of boundaries and the creation of 14 states and six union territories. Language was a major consideration but not the only one in the creation of the states. The creation of the new states continued even after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act. Four years later, Bombay state was split into the Gujarati-speaking Gujarat state and the Marathi-speaking Maharashtra. After persistent demands by the tribes, Nagaland was carved out of Assam state in 1963 because of its distinct language and culture. Indian Punjab was split into three parts, with Punjabi-speaking Punjab, Hindi-speaking Haryana and the hilly northern tracts merged into Himachal. In all, 15 new states were created or upgraded from union territories after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. In the meantime, some areas were downgraded to union territories; the latest such move saw the illegal splitting of Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir into the two ‘union territories’ of Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir in 2019. The latest tally is 28 states and eight union territories. As stated earlier, most of the new states and union territories were created on the basis of identity such as language, ethnicity, culture and geography, or the difference in the level of development in two parts of a state. There is hardly a case where a state was created just because of its large population. Uttar Pradesh, with an estimated population of over 243 million, is a case in point. The state’s population almost matches the population of Pakistan. The population of the US has increased 10 times since 1863, but not a single state has been carved out of the existing ones since then. The last state created this way was West Virginia, which had seceded from Virginia in 1863 during the Civil War. What are the lessons from the two-country case studies above? The first is that population on its own is not enough of a reason to split a province into two or more units. Pakistan’s population has increased four times since 1973, but this alone may not justify the creation of more provinces. There may be merit in the proposal to create more provinces, but such reorganisation should be studied in depth, preferably by a commission or even a parliamentary committee as was done when the 18th Constitutional Amendment was being drafted. The concentration of too many powers in the provinces is a key issue that needs to be addressed. Creating more provinces may not be the best solution for this problem as it will not only be an expensive exercise but may also create political instability in one or more provinces. The problem, in my opinion, may be solved by creating a balance of powers among the three tiers of the state — federal, provincial and local. This balance can be effectively achieved by empowering local government through a comprehensive constitutional amendment, as India did in 1993. The LGs already have elaborate infrastructure and staff, unlike the proposed new provinces. The proposed amendment should not only guarantee adequate powers for various tiers of local government but should also ensure the direct transfer of funds to LGs from the National Finance Commission. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

items.title: The beneficiaries of war
items.description: WARS are generally assessed through a binary lens. Strategic analysts, policymakers and the media tend to focus on a simple question — who won and who lost? The recent US-Iran war has generated a similar debate. Has Washington been able to achieve its objectives? Has Iran successfully withstood American military pressure and preserved its capacity to resist? But this binary framework overlooks another, often more consequential, dimension of modern warfare. Wars do not merely produce military winners and losers. They also redistribute wealth, accelerate technological change and create commercial opportunities for industries positioned to profit from insecurity. In the case of the US-Iran conflict, the most obvious beneficiaries may ultimately be neither Washington nor Tehran. The two capitals have both paid a substantial price. They have expended military resources, suffered economic disruption and experienced varying degrees of tactical and strategic pain. The conflict may therefore produce no clear geopolitical victor. Yet several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners. The foremost beneficiary of the US-Iran conflict has been the defence industry. Modern wars consume extraordinary quantities of missiles, interceptors, drones, precision-guided munitions and other military equipment. Every missile fired has to be replaced. Every depleted stockpile creates new procurement requirements. Every perceived vulnerability generates pressure for additional defence spending. The financial results of major US defence companies illustrate this dynamic. Several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners in the US-Iran conflict. Lockheed Martin reported earnings of $1.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $342 million during the same period in 2025. Its sales increased by 11 per cent to $20.1bn, while its backlog reached a record $230bn. Sales in its missiles and fire control segment increased by 19pc to $4.1bn. Similarly, RTX, the parent company of Raytheon, reported Q2 2026 net income of $2.139bn, up from $1.657bn in the corresponding quarter of 2025. Raytheon sales increased by 18pc to $8.269bn, supported by demand for systems such as Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM. A prolonged conflict not only increases the immediate consumption of weapons but also generates a second wave of demand, ie, replenishment of stockpiles. The conflict between the US and Iran has resultantly become a multi-year procurement cycle for these firms. The longer the insecurity persists, the more governments feel compelled to order additional weapons, ammunition and defensive systems. For the military-industrial complex, geopolitical instability can translate into expanding order books. Select firms in the energy sector have been another major beneficiary. The US-Iran war, combined with uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions to regional energy flows, created precisely the conditions in which large oil companies, refiners and commodity traders tend to thrive on higher prices, supply uncertainty and extreme market volatility. The figures are striking. ExxonMobil’s Q2 2026 net income reached $14.5bn, compared with $7.08bn in the corresponding period of 2025, which is an increase of almost 105 pc. Similarly, Chevron’s earnings increased dramatically, while Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66 and Valero Energy also recorded major gains as higher energy prices and refining margins transformed geopolitical disruption into exceptional financial returns. The trend was not confined to the US. Shell reported Q2 2026 profits of $9.84bn, compared with $4.26bn in Q2 2025, while British Petroleum reported $5.7bn, compared with $2.34bn during the corresponding period. TotalEnergies, Saudi Aramco, Glencore and Trafigura also benefited from the extraordinary volatility created by the conflict and the resulting disruption in energy markets. The point is not that every energy company automatically benefits from every war. Conflict can also destroy infrastructure, disrupt production and create substantial risks. But the US-Iran war demonstrates how supply disruptions and uncertainty can produce extraordinary gains for companies capable of trading volatility, refining crude and exploiting higher prices. For many firms, instability itself can become profitable. The beneficiaries of modern conflict are no longer limited to companies manufacturing tanks and missiles. Warfare is increasingly dependent on artificial intelligence, cloud computing, satellite data, cybersecurity and real-time battlefield analysis. Palantir Technologies has emerged as one of the glaring examples of this transformation. In Q2 2026, the company generated revenue of $1.94bn, representing 93pc year-on-year growth. Revenue from the US government reached $809m, an increase of 90pc. Microsoft also secured a five-year Pentagon contract worth $9.69bn for Microsoft 365, cloud subscriptions and other services for the US military and intelligence community. At the same time, the Pentagon has been pushing AI companies to expand their capabilities into classified networks, creating new opportunities for firms capable of developing secure AI systems for military and intelligence purposes. The US-Iran war may therefore accelerate a structural transformation in the military marketplace. Global shipping industry is another example of war-generated profits. Disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz forced vessels to alter routes and created enormous uncertainty in global shipping markets. The resulting increase in freight rates transformed tanker operations into a highly profitable business. Frontline and Scorpio Tankers are some prominent examples with record Q1 and Q2 earnings of 2026. There are also less visible beneficiaries. Defence consultants, geopolitical risk firms, intelligence service providers, private security contractors and an expanding ecosystem of digital media personalities have all found that geopolitical crises generate unprecedented demand for their products, services and content. Although, decisions on war and peace are determined by governments, it is equally difficult to ignore the political economy associated with prolonged warfare. This raises an uncomfortable question: if war creates exponential profits for some industries, would they prefer the settlement of conflicts or their prolonged continuation? The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own. X: @itskhurramabbas Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026
